documents.text: Equality Impact Assessment What is being assessed Norwich Home Options Allocation Policy Status Assessment of a statutory function update Officer completing this form Graduate Management Trainee Team Home Options Directorate Communities and Housing SLT sponsor Executive director of communities and housing Date assessment commenced 28th October 2025 Date of completion 4th November 2025 Will the report this EqIA relates to go to Committee? Scrutiny Committee (15th January 2025) What are the main aims or purpose of the strategy, policy, plan, project, contract or major change to your service which you are considering? Part 4 of the Housing Act determines that local authorities must have an allocation scheme to determine priorities between applicants for Norwich City Council owned (social) housing and to set out the procedure to be followed when allocating social housing in their area. In Norwich, the allocation scheme is called Home Options. The current Home Options allocations policy dates from October 2021 and needs updating to incorporate new legislation and statutory guidance. The update also presents the opportunity to ensure that policy reflects local needs and issues. This EqIA covers the entire policy, highlighting specific proposed changes to the policy: (a) local connection requirement increased from 6 months to 2 years (b) reduction in permitted social housing refusals from 5 to 3 (c) prioritisation of armed forces veterans on housing shortlists within each band How does it fit with other services and policies, and how does it support our corporate priorities? Revisions to the Housing Allocations policy were developed in parallel with the development of the Norwich Homelessness and Rough Sleeping Strategy (2025–2030). These policy changes are closely aligned with the strategy and support the operational work of the homelessness prevention and relief teams. The revised housing register eligibility and prioritisation criteria will promote social housing allocation to the most vulnerable local people who are engaged with home options, including those at risk of homelessness or who are currently homeless. These policy revisions will influence both who can join the register and how quickly they may be allocated housing. The new housing allocation policy aligns to the “A Fairer Norwich” community-led plan priority: working to support local people and families so that they can face economic and social challenges. The policy aims to reduce inequality and the negative effects of poverty by prioritising social housing allocation for those who are the most in need within our city. What is the reason for the proposal or change (financial, legal etc)? The council has a statutory requirement to review and update their housing allocations policy in line with any significant changes to legislation, local priorities or local needs. In line with the update of the Homelessness and Rough Sleeping strategy (2025-2030), the allocations policy was reviewed and updated. Who will be affected by this strategy, policy, plan, project, contract or major change to your service? (Please tick all that apply) ☒ Residents ☐ Visitors ☐ Council Staff ☐ Businesses ☐ Workers Please state any specific client group or groups Specific groups impacted by this policy are: Norwich City Council social housing tenants Individuals applying for Norwich City Council home options Individuals at risk of homelessness Individuals experiencing homelessness Which wards will be impacted by your proposal? Does your proposal impact any of the council’s Reducing Inequality Target Areas (RITAs)? ☒ ALL Norwich City Council wards ☐ Bowthorpe ☐ Catton Grove ☐ Crome ☐ Eaton ☐ Lakenham ☐ Mancroft ☐ Mile Cross ☐ Nelson ☐ Sewell ☐ Thorpe Hamlet ☐ Town Close ☐ University ☐ Wensum ☒ Catton Grove☒ North City Centre ☒ Earlham ☒ Pilling Park ☒ Heartsease☒ Vauxhall Street ☒ Mid Lakenham ☒ West Pottergate and Russell Street ☒ Mile Cross What outcomes do you want to achieve, why and for who? Norwich has experienced significant population growth over the last decade and is the most densely populated district in Norfolk. Norwich, as with any city, faces some challenges including significant and entrenched inequality and deprivation: the latest data published by the End Child Poverty Coalition shows that between 2023-2024, 35.3% of children in Norwich were living in households below the poverty line. As of October 2025, Norwich City Council owns a total of 14,211 properties, which includes 13,291 general needs homes and 920 sheltered homes. Despite this stock, the 2021 Greater Norwich Housing Needs Assessment projected a significant shortfall in social housing provision. Demand continues to outpace supply, particularly among Home Options applicants who are unable to access the increasingly unaffordable private rental sector. The need for appropriate housing for vulnerable individuals and families is both urgent and well-evidenced. Homelessness is associated with significant health consequences for all experiencing it, including mental illness, infectious disease, heart disease, and early mortality (Crisis UK). Young people experiencing housing instability are more likely to be absent or excluded from school, while parents face heightened risks of depression and anxiety due to housing insecurity (Local Government Association, 2017). Older adults, particularly those over 60, are at increased risk of developing depression and dementia (Local Government Association, 2017). Temporary accommodation (TA) exacerbates these issues: two-thirds of TA residents report its negative impact on their mental and physical health (Shelter, 2023), and children residing in temporary housing for over a year are three times as likely to experience anxiety, depression, and infection compared to their housed peers (Shelter, 2006). Once within the social housing system, household changes can lead to overcrowding; a lack of available, larger homes prevents households from moving, thereby increasing their likelihood of mental illness, sleep disturbance, second-hand tobacco exposure, relationship breakdown, and poor educational attainment for children (WHO, 2018). A lack of stable housing additionally negatively impacts job and educational attainment, perpetuating the factors that entrap individuals in poverty and increase their need for social housing provision to prevent their homelessness (Crisis UK). Certain groups are disproportionately affected by homelessness risk or its negative consequences, including families with children, those who are pregnant, army veterans, care leavers, refugees, those fleeing abuse, those experiencing severe mental illness, and those with complex, multiple needs (St Martin in the Fields UK). To mitigate these harms and prevent homelessness among the most vulnerable through a very limited number of council-owned homes, the Home Options allocation policy must prioritise those in greatest need within Norwich. This prioritisation is primarily guided by statutory and legislative frameworks, supplemented by locally informed criteria that reflect emerging trends and community needs. What evidence and data has been used for this assessment, including community engagement and consultation? The new home options allocation policy will go through numerous stages of consultation and debate before sign-off. The draft policy revisions, alongside its summary report and this EqIA, will be uploaded to Get Talking Norwich for the public to view, to allow engagement and comments from the community. The results of this consultation will be considered before the revised policy is assessed and debated within scrutiny committee. This EqIA will also be revised following public consultation. Amendments and suggestions from scrutiny committee will be implemented as appropriate before the final revised policy will go to the council’s cabinet for sign off. Who implements, carries out or delivers the policy, practice, service or function? The home options, homelessness prevention, and homelessness relief teams. Will anyone be disproportionately affected by what you are proposing, and/or will it create any benefits? Due to additions to revised policy: Populations impacted positively: Armed Forces Veterans Populations with extra support in place to mitigate impact: Refugees Ex-offenders If yes, complete the relevant sections overleaf for any benefits and adverse impacts identified. Affected group Key findings from analysis of data and evidence. Identify any gaps in data here Level & type of impact: Actions to mitigate impacts, maximise benefits or address identified gaps in data By when dd/mm/yy A group defined by age (60+) No specific impact identified N/A N/A N/A N/A Those with physical access or mobility needs Positive Impact: (In line with current Home Options Allocation Policy) Gold priority banding will be awarded to those in severe medical need who need urgent re-housing due to a strongly evidenced, serious and enduring medical condition or disability, which is severely and permanently affected by their current accommodation. This includes those who are housebound through mobility issues and moving to alternative accommodation would alleviate this, and those who have a terminal illness, where alternative accommodation would allow for suitable care to be provided. ☒ Positive impact ☐ Adverse impact ☐ Low impact ☐ Medium impact ☒ High impact N/A – Allocation priority outlined in policy. Ongoing Those that identify as disabled Extra support in place to mitigate impact: (In line with current Home Options Allocation Policy) People with learning disabilities or neurodivergence may face barriers in navigating the application process or understanding eligibility criteria. ☐ Positive impact ☒ Adverse impact ☐ Low impact ☒ Medium impact ☐ High impact Extra support for this group: The council’s Home Options team will continue to support all residents who need help with their housing needs, including those who require information in more accessible formats. We are committed to ensuring that everyone can access housing information in a way that meets their individual communication needs. The Home Options team hold a assisted applicants list for relevant applicants that require further support from the team to ensure they are not disadvantaged by the relative complexity of the Home Options application processes. Ongoing Gender reassignment No specific impact identified N/A N/A N/A N/A Marriage and civil partnership No specific impact identified N/A N/A N/A N/A Pregnancy and maternity No specific impact identified N/A N/A N/A N/A Race/ethnicity No specific impact identified N/A N/A N/A N/A Religion and belief No specific impact identified N/A N/A N/A N/A Sex No specific impact identified N/A N/A N/A N/A Sexual orientation No specific impact identified N/A N/A N/A N/A Socio-economic hardship Positive Impact: (In line with current Home Options Allocation Policy) Norwich has high levels of deprivation, with over a third of children living below the poverty line. Many residents face barriers to accessing private rental housing due to affordability, insecure employment, or benefit restrictions. These groups are disproportionately represented among Home Options applicants. As such, the Home Options team hold an assisted applicants list for relevant applicants that require further support from the team to ensure they are not disadvantaged by the relative complexity of the Home Options application processes. ☒ Positive impact ☐ Adverse impact ☐ Low impact ☒ Medium impact ☐ High impact Overall, the policy aligns with anti-poverty objectives in the council’s community-led plan. Its prioritisation of applicants in greatest housing need supports those experiencing poverty. Ongoing Refugees and Migrants Extra support in place to mitigate impact on this population: (Due to addition to revised policy: (a) local connection requirement increased from 6 months to 2 years) Many asylum seekers are housed in Norwich-based accommodation while awaiting the outcome of their applications. If granted refugee status, they have 28 days to secure permanent housing. Although their residence in Norwich begins upon placement within asylum accommodation, the refugee-application process typically lasts significantly less than the two years required to qualify for the housing register, limiting their options for permanent accommodation upon exit. ☐ Positive impact ☒ Adverse impact ☐ Low impact ☒ Medium impact ☐ High impact Extra support for this group: Norwich City Council has formed a specialist refugee housing team that uses targeted grants to help individuals leaving asylum dispersal accommodation access private rental sector, thereby bypassing the continuous residence requirement for social housing. The council aims to continue to enable the success. provided by the refugee housing specialists. Ongoing Armed Forces (includes those who have served or continue to serve in our Armed Forces) Positive Impact: (In line with current Home Options Allocation Policy) As Norwich City Council has signed the Armed Forces Covenant, people with particular connections to the military don’t need to meet local connection rules when applying for home options. This includes people currently serving or who have served in the regular Armed Forces; bereaved spouses or civil partners who must leave military housing after their partner dies, if the death was related to their service; former reserve force members with serious health issues caused by their service; and divorced or separated spouses or civil partners who are required to leave Ministry of Defence accommodation. Armed forces members and veterans are at a significantly risk of developing illness because of their service, resulting in their increased vulnerability. As such, gold priority banding will be awarded to Armed Forces members and veterans suffering from mental or physical ill health as a result of their service (where this is strongly evidenced, serious and enduring, and is severely and permanently affected by their current accommodation). (Due to addition to revised policy: (c) prioritisation of Armed Forces veterans on shortlists) UK Armed Forces veterans will also have the highest priority within any band they are placed in. On property shortlisting, where there is more than one applicant in the band, the offer will be made to any UK Armed Forces veteran within that band, followed by the applicant who has been waiting the longest within that band. ☒ Positive impact ☐ Adverse impact ☐ Low impact ☐ Medium impact ☒ High impact N/A – Allocation priority outlined in policy. Ongoing. Other groups – Ex Offenders Extra support in place to mitigate impact on this population: (Due to addition to revised policy: local connection requirement increased from 6 months to 2 years) Housing ex-offenders upon their release from prison, alongside providing holistic support services, has been shown to reduce re-offending rates by 50% (Department of Levelling Up, Housing and Communities, 2023). It is important to note, however, that there is insufficient evidence to show that housing alone produces this effect (Ministry of Justice Analytical Series, 2025). Home Options eligibility requirements restrict ex-offenders from accessing social housing in two ways. Under the Home Options allocations policy, individuals detained in Norwich-based prisons, bail hostels, or approved premises do not gain a local connection to the area through residing in these premises. Ex-offenders additionally face exclusion from Home Options based on behaviour-based criteria including histories of anti-social behaviour, domestic violence, and convictions for violent crime. ☐ Positive impact ☒ Adverse impact ☐ Low impact ☒ Medium impact ☐ High impact Extra support for this group: A homelessness prevention referral can be made to the council by the probation service 8 weeks before an individual is released from prison, where work can begin to prevent their homelessness upon release. This mitigates the need for the applicant to present to the council themselves. Several housing alternatives are available to ex-offenders, including supported accommodation and private rentals. Norwich City Council has developed a specialist ex-offender housing team that utilises the Accommodation for Ex-Offenders (AfEO) fund (a central government fund that helps local authorities provide stable housing and support for individuals leaving prison, thereby reducing homelessness and connected reoffending rates) to help them secure residence within the private rented sector. Since 2023, 91 ex-offenders have been housed through this approach. AfEO funding will end in April 2026, but the council aims to continue the success provided by the ex-offender housing specialists. Applicants excluded from Home Options if based on behaviour-based criteria may re-gain access if they can demonstrate that they have addressed these issues, as outlined in sections 5.0.4 and 5.0.5 of the policy. Ongoing. Other groups – Care Leavers Positive impact: (In line with current Home Options Allocation Policy) Care leavers aged 18-21 years (or up to 25 years old if they are pursuing a programme of education agreed in their pathway plan) that are assessed as ‘needing to move on’ bypass the local connection requirements and are awarded gold priority banding, subject to criteria. ☒ Positive impact ☐ Adverse impact ☐ Low impact ☐ Medium impact ☒ High impact N/A – Allocation priority outlined in policy. Ongoing Other groups – those fleeing domestic abuse Positive impact: (In line with current Home Options Allocation Policy) Policy provides local connection exceptions and gold priority banding when safety needs are verified. ☒ Positive impact ☐ Adverse impact ☐ Low impact ☐ Medium impact ☒ High impact N/A – Allocation priority outlined in policy. Ongoing Other groups – those living in overcrowded accommodation Positive impact: (In line with current Home Options Allocation Policy) Gold priority banding will be awarded to applicants lacking two or more bedrooms. Silver priority banding will be awarded to applicants lacking one bedroom and those verified as ‘sofa surfing’. ☒ Positive impact ☐ Adverse impact ☐ Low impact ☐ Medium impact ☒ High impact N/A – Allocation priority outlined in policy. Other groups – those at risk of homelessness, those who are homeless, and those who are rough sleeping Positive Impact: (In line with current Home Options Allocation Policy) Where the council has accepted a homelessness prevention or relief duty for an applicant who does not hold a priority need, such applicants will be awarded a silver priority banding, subject to criteria. Applicants who are verified to be sleeping rough will be awarded silver priority banding, subject to criteria. ☒ Positive impact ☐ Adverse impact ☐ Low impact ☒ Medium impact ☐ High impact N/A – Allocation priority outlined in policy. Other groups – families with young children Positive Impact: (In line with current Home Options Allocation Policy) Applicants with dependent children under the age of 10 who live in a flat or maisonette that does not have its own private outdoor space are awarded silver priority banding. Households that include children aged six or under, who live in a property on the third floor or above where there is no lift access, will move up one further priority band. ☒ Positive impact ☐ Adverse impact ☐ Low impact ☒ Medium impact ☐ High impact N/A – Allocation priority outlined in policy. Are there any negative impacts that cannot reasonably be avoided? Increasing the local connection requirement to two years will impact recent arrivals, refugees, and people placed in prison who return to Norwich. The change is a government guideline-based decision that prioritises limited social housing for long‑term local residents. Targeted mitigations will be provided, such as continued refugee private rental support, ex‑offender private rental support, and exception routes and enhanced priority banding for care leavers, domestic abuse victims and army veterans. How has the equality impact assessment informed or changed the proposal? This EqIA has highlighted the key groups likely to be affected by the policy and reinforced the need for the continuation of the services which work to mitigate these impacts. These include the specialist rental support teams for refugees and ex-offenders. What actions have been identified going forward? Moving forward, the council will: Continue to fund and support the Refugee Housing Team to help refugees leaving asylum accommodation access private rented housing. Aim to sustain the positive outcomes achieved by Accommodation for Ex-Offenders (AfEO) team within the Home Options team beyond April 2026 when AfEO central government funding ends. Maintain the assisted applicants list and carry out regular outreach to ensure vulnerable residents receive appropriate support. How will the impact of your proposal and actions be measured moving forward? Review of allocation policy impact 1 year from implementation (February 2027) Negative outcomes action plan: Actions identified from EqIA Target completion date (dd/mm/yy) Responsible Officer (role) Comments Action complete Continue and resource Refugee Housing Team Private Rental Sector grants to house refugees leaving asylum accommodation. Ongoing Home Options Manager ☐ Aim to sustain the positive outcomes achieved by Accommodation for Ex-Offenders (AfEO) team within the Home Options team beyond April 2026 when AfEO central government funding ends. 01/04/2026 Home Options Manager ☐ Maintain assisted applicants list and regular outreach to vulnerable applicants. Ongoing Home Options Manager ☐ For the assessment to be final, the relevant people agreeing it must sign it off below. documents.title: Scrutiny Minutes 15 January 2026
documents.text: MINUTES Scrutiny Committee 16:30 to 18:35 Thursday, 15 January 2026 Present: Councillors Wright (Chair), Galvin (Vice-Chair), Champion, Fulton- McAlister, Hoechner, Kendrick, Lawes, Oliver, Sands (S), Sands (M), Stutely Apologies: Councillor Smith In attendance: Councillor Jones, Cabinet Member for Housing Davina Howes, Executive Director of Communities and Housing Chris Haystead, Housing Options Manager Andrew Turnbull, Development Strategy Manager Robert Carmichael, Democratic Services Manager Charlotte McCalister, Housing Partnerships Officer Amy Nagle, Graduate Management Trainee (Communities and Housing) 43. Declarations of Interest 43.1 Councillor Stutely declared an other registerable interest as a former Non- Executive Director of Lion Homes, which was relevant to Item 46, Housing Development at Mile Cross Depot Site. 44. Minutes 44.1 RESOLVED that the public and exempt minutes of the meeting held on 18 December 2025 were confirmed and signed as a true record. 44.2 The Chair invited Councillor Galvin, the Committee’s representative on the Norfolk Health Overview Select Committee (NHOSC), to provide a brief update on the most recent meeting of the Committee, which took place on 15 January 2026. Councillor Galvin updated Members on the following items: MINUTES • Eastern Pathology Alliance (EPA) Weekend Pathology Testing – East Norfolk Medical Practice addressed the Committee about the decision to stop weekend pathology testing. The ICB had explained that its Equalities Impact Assessment had not identified the problems around stopping the service. A report would go to the Committee again at a later date. The Committee had agreed to write to Councillor Graham Plant, Cabinet Member for Highways, Infrastructure and Transport at Norfolk County Council, to ask him to provide a report on bus transport to hospitals. • Palliative and End of Life Care – The ICB had completed a large review, as had Marie Curie. Reports identified that provision was inconsistent and inequitable across Norfolk. A new service specification was being developed for end-of-life care. • Norfolk Medicines Support Service – The ICB were due to stop the service as the funding for the service had ended. The Committee had asked Norfolk County Council to explain the decision to end the funding and wanted more information on the impact of stopping the service. • Forward Work Programme – Several items which impacted Norwich would be discussed in future meetings. This included a strategic review of outreach services, including the Wellness on Wheels bus, which would be pre-scrutinised. The Committee were also informed that the contracts let by the ICB were called in to the Secretary of State for Health and Social Care. There were concerns about who the contracts had been awarded to, which were raised at the meeting. 44.3 Councillor Galvin encouraged Members of the Committee to reach out to her if they wanted to know more about NHOSC. 45. Revisions to the Home Options Policy 45.1 The Cabinet Member for Housing thanked the Scrutiny Committee for the opportunity to present the proposed revisions to the Home Options policy. 45.2 The Housing Options Manager explained that the Council had undertaken consultation and changes to the policy were driven by new legislation and statutory guidance that the Council needed to follow. He highlighted the proposed changes to the policy, which included: • All applications would involve a discussion of an applicant’s housing need with an advisor. • Applicants must have been continuously resident in Norwich for at least the last two years, in accordance with statutory guidance and to ensure MINUTES that the Council’s housing policies benefited local people, with some exceptions. • The number of refusals allowed before an application was cancelled for 12 months would be reduced from five to three to reflect the high demand for social housing. • Clarification of priority banding for rough sleepers. Where it was confirmed that an applicant was sleeping rough, met the qualification criteria and had no other accommodation available to them, the silver band would be awarded by the Council’s rough sleeper team. • UK armed forces veterans would be prioritised within bands, in accordance with the Armed Forces Covenant. 45.3 The Housing Options Manager explained that the proposed changes had been subject to consultation. 72 responses had been received and were detailed in the report. The Chair thanked the Housing Options Manager for the introduction and noted that 72 responses was an improvement on previous years. 45.4 A Member asked for more information about the special circumstances in which an applicant would not need to have been a continuous resident in Norwich for at least the previous two years. In response, the Housing Options Manager clarified there were several special circumstances, such as those fleeing domestic violence, where applicants did not need to evidence continuous residence. 45.5 In response to a Member’s question, the Housing Options Manager explained that in terms of Council accommodation, the only properties that were not able to accept large pets were tower blocks. 45.6 Discussion ensued on households. The Housing Options Manager clarified that the Council would not consider relatives who did not form part of the applicant’s immediate family where there was no formal care arrangement as part of the applicant’s household. This included parents or step-parents, grandparents, siblings or step-siblings, aunts, uncles, grandchildren, nieces, nephews or cousins. The Housing Options Manager explained that anyone outside of the immediate family was excluded as demand was high and prioritisation was necessary. The Cabinet Member for Housing added that given the large demand, the Council sought to free up larger properties and help people to downsize where appropriate. She noted that the need for larger properties was significant, and the Council needed to be realistic about the availability of larger houses and meet the needs of the most vulnerable. 45.7 In response to a Member’s question, the Housing Options Manager explained that the Council had an arrangement with Dog’s Trust for pet fostering. 45.8 Discussion ensued on the housing need bands as detailed in the report. A Member was concerned housing arrangements did not facilitate shared custody of children and that children would be penalised for their parents’ MINUTES decision making. The Housing Options Manager explained that there was not enough housing available to enable an applicant to have a spare bedroom that was vacant, for example, when their child was staying with their other parent. He emphasised that there were families who needed extra rooms permanently and the system sought to prioritise greatest need. Housing benefit issues also had to be considered. 45.9 A Member queried how applicants with changing care arrangements, such as fostering children, were considered. The Housing Options Manager explained that the policy stated if someone was fostering or in a foster arrangement, their household would be amended once it was evidenced to officers. He assured Members that the Housing team would support them to find a suitable arrangement. 45.10 A Member asked officers to clarify which revisions to the policy were driven by legislation. The Housing Options Manager explained that the addition of the realistic conversation and the reduction in number of refusals were Council additions, and the remaining changes were due to guidance and legislation. 45.11 In response to a Member’s question, the Housing Options Manager informed Members that the Council had undertaken a publicity drive as part of the Norfolk Armed Forces Covenant Board, to better publicise services for veterans. 45.12 A Member sought assurance that the honest and realistic conversations that the Housing team had with applicants were guided by trauma-informed care practices. She noted that she had worked with residents who hadn’t been able to complete the process for personal reasons and had been daunted by the prospect of starting the process again. The Housing Options Manager explained that the Council sought to humanise the process by talking to applicants at the beginning and providing them with advice. He added that the Council was part of a trauma-informed practice working group and took a person-centred approach to working with different clients. 45.13 Discussion ensued on the Assessment Panel, which was referenced throughout the report. A Member questioned who was on the Panel and requested more information on their decision-making process. The Committee agreed that they would like to see that information outlined within the policy. Officers agreed to provide that information within the policy. 45.14 Discussion continued on the implications of the policy on joint-custody households. The Executive Director of Communities and Housing explained that the Council’s approach was standard. The Cabinet Member for Housing added that the policy took a realistic approach. Members asked officers to complete some analysis on co-parenting in Council-owned properties. The Executive Director of Communities and Housing agreed that research was likely already available from the housing and voluntary sector which officers would draw on and present back to the Scrutiny Committee at a later date. MINUTES 45.15 A Member proposed that they would like to ask Cabinet to remove paragraph 3.8.73 from the policy. The Executive Director of Communities and Housing explained that the point was about the housing band priority, and it did not prevent families from bidding for a change in property to suit their new circumstances. Several Members stated that the line in the policy was poorly worded and by a majority vote, agreed to ask Cabinet to consider removing the paragraph from the policy. 45.16 RESOLVED, by a majority vote, to: 1. Note the proposed policy changes and make any recommendations to Cabinet before its approval and adoption of a new Home Options policy. 2. Ask Cabinet to consider removing paragraph 3.8.7.3 from the proposed policy. 45.17 RESOLVED to note the following actions: 1. To include more information about the Assessment Panel in the policy, including the make up of the panel, its governance and decision-making processes and circulate this information to the Scrutiny Committee. 2. Request that officers explore research from national organisations and others regarding the impact co-parenting in Council-owned properties, needs of families and impact and provide a brief update at a future Scrutiny Committee meeting. 46. Housing Development at Mile Cross Depot Site 46.1 The Cabinet Member for Housing introduced the report. She explained that the development at Mile Cross Depot Site had been an interesting and complex process, and much time had been spent on making the site fit for purpose. She informed Members that the Council was continuously seeking opportunities to add to its housing stock. 46.2 The Development Strategy Manager explained that the report outlined the history of the site over the previous 5-7 years. The site had significant ground issues, notably demolished former dwellings and rubble deposited on the site, contamination across the site, a main sewage pipe to the northern boundary and peat to the southern boundary. He reminded Members that the Covid-19 pandemic and introduction of Nutrient Neutrality had also affected the development of the site. 46.3 The Development Strategy Manager explained that since the ground civilisation works were completed at the end of 2023/early 2024, there had been significant progression, with the planning application submitted in February 2024 and approved in November 2024. A decision was taken to do an early stage enabling package of works to de-risk future phases of the MINUTES development. The contractor was working on Stage 1 and a pre-construction services agreement. A detailed cost plan would be developed to give cost certainty in the summer of 2026. 46.4 The Chair thanked officers for the update and opened the discussion to questions. 46.5 In response to a Member’s question, the Development Strategy Manager clarified that there would be 67 new affordable homes developed on the site. He also explained that a new bell mouth entrance to the site would be constructed for residents. 46.6 Discussion ensued on Local Government Reorganisation (LGR). A Member sought assurance that the development would not be delayed or disrupted due to LGR. The Executive Director of Communities and Housing explained that the Government had made it clear that spending on the Housing Revenue Account (HRA) needed to continue given its importance and the needs of running a housing service. A Member asked whether precautions were in place to prevent a loss of institutional knowledge should there be a high turnover of Council officers due to LGR. The Executive Director of Communities and Housing stated that there needed to be clear governance and business continuity throughout the transition period. She added that information was shared across centralised folders that officers had access to for business continuity. From a resource perspective, the Development Strategy Manager added that his team had secured a new Senior Development Officer in October 2025 and additional interim resource for Mile Cross, demonstrating that the Council retained the ability to recruit. 46.7 A Member noted that the Mile Cross site was nearby Sweet Briar marshes, which had become a significant urban wildlife reserve, the Marriott’s Way cycle route and the River Wensum and asked how the site would be integrated in the landscape. The Development Strategy Manager responded that a positive of the development was the way it opened up to the Marriott’s Way. He explained that there would be connections through to the Marriot’s Way and increased lines of visibility across Mile Cross Road to Marriott’s Way. 46.8 In response to a Member’s question, the Development Strategy Manager explained that there would be no gas in any new developments going forward. The Cabinet Member for Housing added that there had been discussions about communal battery storage which she would revisit. 46.9 A Member thanked officers for their work on the brownfield site, noting the difficulty that it presented. He sought assurance that there would not be delays on other brownfield sites under development. The Development Strategy Manager explained that whilst he could not predict what would be found under the ground, mitigation measures were in place. He explained that learning from the Mile Cross development had been applied to the Argyle Street scheme and overall, officers recognised that it was appropriate to MINUTES spend more time up front de-risking the site, to increase likely contractors who would price competitively. 46.10 The Development Strategy Manager detailed learning that had emerged as part of the development of Mile Cross. He explained that he recognised the need to take people on a journey, help them understand the indicative programme of activities and potentially break the development down into phases. There had also been discussions on how to communicate developments with residents and the wider community, including sharing more visual information and regular updates. The Chair agreed that that approach would embed more public confidence and understanding. The Cabinet Member for Housing added that the Housing Hub and the housing updates which she circulated to all Councillors formed part of that effort. 46.11 In response to a Member’s question, the Cabinet Member for Housing clarified that the Mile Cross development site was always planned to be a HRA site. She explained that the Council wanted to build as much social housing as possible across the City, however, needed to consider multiple sites, competing priorities and capital costs. The focus for Mile Cross was to deliver 67 affordable homes and then consider next steps. The Cabinet Member for Housing explained that competing demands needed to be balanced. The Development Strategy Manager added that the Social and Affordable Homes Programme (SAHP) had been released by Homes England and the Council were exploring the opportunities that that change would bring. 46.12 A Member noted that of the 1,008 new houses completed in the City since 2020, 291 were affordable homes. 262 of those 291 were enabled or delivered by the Council, meaning that only 29 affordable units were delivered by private developers. The Development Strategy Manager explained that the Council had provided grants of right to buy receipts through the Section 106 system and was responsible for the majority of affordable housing either through direct delivery on site or by working with partners A Member commented that that was a concern, but noted that LGR might give the Council more potential outside of the current City boundaries. 46.13 The Committee agreed to recommend that subsequent phases were presented to Scrutiny for pre-Scrutiny before going to Cabinet. 46.14 A Member was pleased to note that air-source heat pumps and solar panels were to be included in the development and the Committee agreed to ask Cabinet to consider adding battery storage and electric car changing as standard across the site. 46.15 Discussion ensued on community engagement. A Member noted that community engagement needed to be embedded within the development and proposed that communities be given opportunities to provide input in the Marriott’s Way amelioration work and into the hoardings around the site. The Development Strategy Manager advised that the Marriott’s Way was owned by Norfolk County Council, meaning there would need to be liaison with the Council. MINUTES 46.16 Members thanked officers for their work on the development and were pleased to see that the Council continued to develop houses in challenging circumstances. 46.17 RESOLVED to: 1. Note the report. 2. Request that Scrutiny Committee have the opportunity to pre-scrutinise subsequent phases of the Mile Cross development site prior to Cabinet decisions. 3. Commend that there is solar on the site and air source heat pumps. 4. Ask that Cabinet consider adding battery storage and electric car charging as standard across the site. 5. Ask officers to liaise with Norfolk County Council and local community groups to identify wider opportunities for amelioration of the Marriott’s Way as part of the development. 6. Ask that communities have the opportunity to provide input and engage with the hoardings. 47. Nutrient Neutrality Review Scope 47.1 The Chair introduced the item. He explained that in May 2025, the Audit Committee resolved to ‘request that Scrutiny Committee considers reviewing the current position around Nutrient Neutrality and the mitigations’. The Scrutiny Committee agreed to put the item on their Work Programme and agree to key points that they wanted officers to address in the report. These were: • Context about Nutrient Neutrality, it’s introduction and the Council’s response. • Lessons learned regarding the credit scheme. • The effectiveness of Nutrient Neutrality regulations. • The effectiveness of mitigation strategies. • The Council’s work with other authorities. • The impact of nutrients on the River Wensum. • Assurance that further legislation is considered in a timely manner. • Value for money of nutrient credit schemes. 47.2 RESOLVED to request Democratic Services to share the Committee’s key points with officers so that they may draft a report for Scrutiny Committee. 48. Work Programme MINUTES 48.1 A Member requested to add an interim report from the task and finish group, ‘Enhancing Deliberative Democracy and Citizen Participation in Decision- Making’ to the March meeting of the Scrutiny Committee. 48.2 The Chair reminded Members of the Scrutiny Committee to attend Budget Scrutiny training on 29 January 2026. 48.3 RESOLVED to: 1) Add an interim report from the task and finish group, ‘Enhancing Deliberative Democracy and Citizen Participation in Decision-Making’ to the March meeting of the Scrutiny Committee. 2) Agree the Work Programme. CHAIR

documents.topic: Housing allocations (who gets a council home, and in what order)
documents.title: Revisions to the Home Options Policy
documents.text: orwich City Council logo Committee name: Cabinet Committee date: 11/02/2026 Report title: Revisions to the Home Options Policy Portfolio: Councillor Jones, Cabinet Member for Housing Report from: Director of communities and housing Wards: All wards OPEN PUBLIC ITEM Purpose To propose changes to the Council’s social housing allocations policy to incorporate new legislation and statutory guidance. Recommendation: Cabinet is asked to agree the adoption of an updated Home Options policy. Policy framework The Council has five corporate priorities, which are: • An open and modern Council. • A prosperous Norwich. • A fairer Norwich. • A climate responsive Norwich. • A future-proof Norwich. • This report meets the ‘A fairer Norwich’ corporate priority Background 1. Part VI of the Housing Act determines that local authorities must have an allocation scheme to determine priorities between applicants for social housing and to set out the procedure to be followed when allocating social housing in their area. In Norwich, the allocation scheme is called Home Options. 2. The current Home Options allocations policy (Norwich Home Options Allocation Scheme | Norwich City Council) dates from October 2021 and needs updating to incorporate new legislation and statutory guidance. The update also presents the opportunity to ensure that policy reflects local needs and issues. 3. The proposed policy changes, while minimal, take into account legislative changes, statutory guidance (Providing social housing for local people - GOV.UK) as well as the recently published ’National Plan to End Homelessness’ and Government Homelessness Strategy (A National Plan to End Homelessness - GOV.UK). 4. The proposed changes have recently been subject to public consultation and consideration by the Overview and Scrutiny Committee. 5. The draft revised policy is attached at Appendix A. For ease of reference, the proposed changes are highlighted in the policy and detailed below in paragraphs 7 to 11. 6. An Equality Impact Assessment has been undertaken and is attached as Appendix B. Proposed changes to policy 7. All applications will involve a discussion of an applicant’s housing need with an adviser. Applicants who do not meet the criteria for a priority banding category are extremely unlikely to be rehoused through the Home Options scheme and will be given advice about alternative housing options. 8. In accordance with statutory guidance, and to ensure that the council’s housing policies benefit local people, applicants must have been continuously resident in Norwich for at least the last two years. Exceptions, as set down in legislation, will apply. 9. The number of refusals allowed before an application is cancelled for 12 months will be reduced from five to three to reflect extremely high demand for social housing. This will not apply to homelessness clients, who, as required by legislation, receive one offer. 10. Clarification of priority banding for rough sleepers: where it has been confirmed that an applicant is sleeping rough, meets the qualification criteria and it has been assessed that there is no other accommodation available to them, silver band will be awarded by the council’s rough sleeper team. The team will carry out a needs-led assessment and use professional judgement to engage and support people sleeping rough in each case. Priority will not be awarded when the client does not engage with the council’s support or where accommodation has been made available to the applicant which they have chosen not to accept. 11. In accordance with the Armed Forces Covenant, U.K. armed forces veterans will be prioritised within bands. Consultation 12. The Home Options policy public consultation took place between 10 November and 12 December 2025. An online survey was hosted on Get Talking Norwich, the council’s consultation and engagement platform. 13. A dedicated project page was created for the consultation which, which included a narrative, the survey, and the Home Options draft policy, Equality Impact Assessment and briefing note. The consultation was additionally shared with relevant stakeholders via email. 14. Key partners were contacted directly and the proposals were taken to a service users group. 15. A total of 72 responses were received. 16. Responses showed broad agreement (see Appendix C) for all proposals and will be published, along with council comments, in an online report. Consultation key comments 17. In terms of local connection, a respondent raised concerns that people without local connection will remain in hostels longer, blocking move-on pathways. 18. However, this concern can be mitigated as the Council’s hostel move-on agreement with supported accommodation providers sets out how the partners will explore alternative housing and reconnection options for residents without a local connection to Norwich, to ensure that people are supported into housing. 19. In regard to armed forces prioritisation, a respondent raised concerns that concerns that veterans may be prioritised over people with disabilities, domestic abuse survivors, or those in unsafe housing, who may be in greater need of accommodation. 20. However, the prioritisation of armed forces members is in alignment with the requirements of the Armed Forces Covenant, to which the council is signatory. 21. In terms of the clarification of the circumstances by which priority banding for rough sleepers will be awarded, several respondents raised that this banding may act as an incentive to individuals to sleep rough to be verified to receive silver priority banding. 22. In response to this concern and to mitigate such a risk, and in accordance with the National Plan to End Homelessness, we have amended the policy proposal to include a needs-led assessment and the use of professional judgement prior to the award of priority banding. Scrutiny Committee recommendation 23. At Scrutiny Committee on 15 January 2026, the Committee suggested no changes to the proposed amendments to policy (as set out in paragraphs 7 to 11 above). 24. However, Scrutiny Committee did resolve to ask that Cabinet consider removing section 3.8.7.3 of the existing policy from the new policy. 25. Section 3.8.7 of policy sets out that silver band will be awarded where a household has a child aged 10 or under in a flat or maisonette with no private garden. Section 3.8.7.3 sets out that silver band will not be awarded for those children who were born when the current property was accepted. 26. The recommendation from the Scrutiny Committee has been considered by the Portfolio Holder but is not accepted 27. The Portfolio Holder considers that section 3.8.7.3 should remain as now. This policy is designed to ensure that priority banding is not awarded where an applicant’s housing circumstances have been created through their own decisions and choices, for example where an applicant with a child moves into a property with no garden and then applies for priority banding on the grounds that the property is therefore unsuitable. 28. Applicants in such circumstances are able to seek alternative options to resolve their situation, for example, through mutual exchange. Implications 29. There are no proposals in this report that would reduce or increase resources 30. The proposals set out in the report ensure that the council’s allocations policy meet legislative requirements, statutory guidance and government strategy. Other Options Considered 31. No other options have been considered Reasons for the recommendation 32. The current allocations policy is out of date and needs to be amended to include the latest legislation and statutory guidance. The update also presents the opportunity to ensure that policy reflects local needs and issues. Appendices: A: Proposed 2026 Home Options policy B: Equality Impact Assessment C: Consultation response data Contact officer: Name: C Haystead Telephone number: 989405 Email address: chrishaystead@norwich.gov.uk If you would like this agenda in an alternative format, such as a larger or smaller font, audio or Braille, or in a different language, please contact the committee officer above. Appendix A - Proposed 2026 Home Options policy 1. Introduction 1.1.1. This allocation policy explains the rules that determine how Norwich City Council (known throughout this document as ‘the council’) allocates social housing properties. It sets out the priorities and procedures that the council will follow in the letting of social housing to applicants on its housing register. 1.1.2. The Registered Providers (Housing Associations) that are part of the scheme are known throughout this document as ‘scheme landlords’. These are listed in Appendix D. 1.2. Background 1.2.1. The allocation scheme is also known as Home Options. Under the scheme, the council and scheme landlords advertise their properties for rent on a weekly basis on its website and invite bids on each property from applicants who are registered with the scheme. 1.2.2. Norwich is an area of very high housing need and demand for social housing far exceeds the supply of accommodation that becomes available. It must be remembered that Home Options does not produce any more affordable housing but provides a fairer, more efficient and transparent way of allocating the social housing available 1.3. Scheme objectives 1.3.1. The key objectives of the scheme are to: • Meet the legal requirements for the allocation of social housing. • Focus resources on those in the most need. • Operate a scheme which is, fair, transparent and easy to use. • Help meet the housing needs of Norwich residents • Allow scheme users, through the transparent nature of the scheme, to make informed decisions about their housing options. • Make best use of Norwich’s social housing stock. • Encourage and support, balanced and sustainable communities. • Prevent homelessness and reduce the use of temporary accommodation • Encourage through flow from hostel accommodation in order to reduce rough sleeping. • Operate the scheme so that it improves accessibility and customer service for vulnerable groups in Norwich. • Make sure those who have the greatest need for housing have the greatest opportunity to get it • Pay due regard to the aims of the Norwich Homelessness Strategy and Tenancy Strategy • Meet the council’s corporate priorities of ensuring a fairer city 1.4. Legal framework 1.4.1. This allocation scheme complies with the legal framework for allocating social housing, laid down in the Housing Act 1996 and takes account of statutory government guidance on the allocation of accommodation. 1.4.2. This allocation scheme pays due regard to the Equality Act 2010. 1.4.3. The assessment of eligibility, qualification and assessment of priority for the Home Options scheme will take into account any changes to legislation made subsequent to this policy. 1.5. How does the scheme work? 1.5.1. Home Options is a choice-based lettings scheme. The council and scheme landlords advertise their vacant properties to those on the housing register. The adverts include a detailed description of the property. Applicants on the register can then bid for the property of their choice if they are eligible and meet the qualifying criteria. 1.5.2. The successful applicant will be selected from those who have bid for the property and meet the stated qualifying criteria. Selection will be based on the highest band, followed by the banding date where there is more than one applicant from the same band. 1.5.3. Feedback will be provided on what demand there was for previously advertised properties. This will help applicants to make informed choices. 1.5.4. This policy is available free of charge at the website www.norwich.gov.uk. A paper copy of the full policy is available upon request from City Hall at a cost of £25.00. 2. Application Procedure 2.1. How to apply 2.1.1. To apply for a social housing property in Norwich an applicant must be registered with Home Options. 2.1.2. Applications to Home Options can be made over the telephone on 0344 980 3333. All applications will involve a discussion of an applicant’s housing need with an adviser. Acceptance onto Home Options register is not a guarantee that an applicant will be offered accommodation. Home- Options is unable to meet the needs of all home-seekers and transferring tenants looking for accommodation. Applicants who do not meet the criteria for a priority banding category are extremely unlikely to be rehoused through the Home Options scheme and will be given advice about alternative housing options. 2.1.3. Home Options is a scheme which is based on verification. All applicants will be required to provide evidence of their household circumstances including income, savings and housing history. 2.1.4. Information to support an application may be asked for at any time. If the information is not provided, the application may be suspended or removed from Home-Options and any offers of accommodation withdrawn. All applicants will be offered help and advice to complete their application. This includes translation and interpreting facilities where required. 2.2. Who can apply? 2.2.1. Residents of the UK who are over 18 years old can apply to Home Options however this does not guarantee an application will be taken or that the applicant will be re-housed under the scheme. 2.2.2. By law, there are defined groups of applicants who cannot be re-housed through the scheme. There are also exceptions or restrictions to an application which may apply. 2.2.3. Under the Housing Act 1996, local authorities must consider whether applicants are eligible for housing assistance. The council will apply the relevant legislation that is in place at the time of application. 2.3. The applicant’s household 2.3.1. The council will decide in each case as to whether the people included in the application by the applicant will be considered as a part of the household for purposes of assessing housing need. 2.3.2. Any person wishing to be included as part of an applicant’s household must satisfy the Council that they are a permanent member of the applicant’s household and show that it is reasonable to expect them to reside with the applicant on a continuing basis. 2.3.3. The council will not consider the following as members of an applicant’s household: • Anyone who falls within legislation prohibiting them from having recourse to public funds or is an asylum seeker • Non-dependent children who have not lived within the household continually throughout their adult lives • Relatives who do not form part of the applicant’s immediate family where there is no formal care arrangement; parents or step-parents, grandparents, brothers or step-brothers, sisters or step-sisters, aunts, uncles, grandchildren, nieces, nephews, cousins. • Any family member not resident in the UK at the time of the application. • Any person who does not meet eligibility criteria • Friends and acquaintances • Lodgers • Live in help • Students living away from home with their own rent liability 2.3.4. Only dependent children that form a permanent part of the household can be considered. Only if an applicant is evidenced to have their child stay with them for four or more nights a week can they be classed as part of the applicant’s household when making an assessment. Temporary arrangements or contact arrangements cannot be considered and household size will be determined upon evidence that any living arrangements are permanent, and the applicant can demonstrate to the council’s satisfaction that they have full-time, permanent responsibility for the child. Where a formal residence agreement is not in place, the council will consider: • Confirmation from the Courts regarding residency or parental responsibility. • Who the children usually live with • Who has financial responsibility for the children • The length of time any arrangement has been in place • Where the children go to school • Any other relevant information 2.3.5. In cases where an applicant wishes to include their children in their Home Options application, this will not be considered where those children have adequate accommodation available to them elsewhere, for example with another parent. 2.3.6. Household members can only appear on one Home Options application. 2.3.7. Households that have been accepted to adopt or foster a child will be assessed as if they have assumed parental responsibility upon written confirmation from Norfolk County Council being provided. 2.3.8. Where an applicant feels that an additional bedroom is needed for a carer, this can only be considered where we have evidence of the need for permanent 24 hour care from a non-family member who is not part of your household and requires their own bedroom to sleep in on a continuing basis. ‘Waking care’ will not be taken into consideration. We would expect that the applicant would be in receipt of Carer’s Allowance and Disability Living Allowance/Personal Independent Payment with the highest care/enhanced rate component. The carer must be recognised, employed by, or working on behalf of Adult Social Care and we would expect them to be a named person (unless your care is provided on a rota arrangement made by Adult Social Care or an agency on their behalf). The decision will be made by the assessment panel. 2.3.9. Where the family unit is not currently residing together, the assessment will be based on the part of the household that occupies accommodation that provides them with the most suitable housing providing there is a reasonable expectation that they should reside together. 2.3.10. Where an applicant has been assessed in accordance with the Mental Capacity Act 2005 as being unable to hold or to manage a tenancy, they may be suspended from the register until a suitable advocate is appointed to act on their behalf. 2.3.11. For an applicant to become a tenant and enter into a tenancy agreement, they must have the mental capacity to understand the contract. If an applicant does not have the capacity to understand the contract, an application should be made to the Court of Protection by an advocate for the tenancy agreement to be signed on their behalf. 2.3.12. Unborn children will not be considered as part of the assessment. A child cannot be added to an application until the applicant has provided a copy of the birth certificate. 2.3.13. For people in prison, applications can be made within 8 weeks of release if the client meets qualification and local connection criteria. In such instances the client does not need to apply for housing in person and applications will be accepted from a third party on behalf of a person in custody, for example by a Prison Resettlement Officer as part of a Resettlement Plan where third-party consent has been given. 2.3.14. Only household members that meet the eligibility and qualification criteria set out in this policy will be included in an application. 2.4. Eligibility 2.4.1. The Home Options team will determine the eligibility of an applicant, based on immigration status and habitual residence, by applying the legislation that is in place at the time of the application and the point of allocation. 2.4.2. Eligibility for Home Options depends on where the applicant normally lives (‘habitual residence’) and their immigration status. A person is not eligible if they are: • subject to immigration control (with limited exceptions) • classed as an ineligible person from abroad • A person not habitually resident in the United Kingdom or required to leave the UK by the Secretary of State. 2.4.3. Eligibility is explained in detail within statutory guidance – “Allocation of Accommodation: guidance for local authorities” which is online at: Allocation of accommodation: guidance for local authorities - Guidance - GOV.UK (www.gov.uk). 2.4.4. Eligibility for housing assistance can be affected if there is a change in the immigration status of the applicant(s), and therefore eligibility for an allocation of housing will be kept under review. The applicant is responsible for informing the council of any change in their immigration status. 2.4.5. Applicants whose households include a person from abroad who is ineligible will not be afforded priority if they are only homeless or in housing need as a consequence of the presence of the ineligible person. 2.5. Qualification for housing in Norwich 2.5.1. The Localism Act 2011 allows councils to make local decisions about who qualifies for social housing in their area in order to ensure that local objectives and the needs of local residents are met. 2.5.2. The decision that an applicant does not qualify for an allocation may occur at the time of joining the Home Options scheme, at any time during the life of the application, at the time the applicant is allocated a property, or when the applicant has bid and has been short-listed for a property. The Home Options team will make the decision. 2.5.3. In accordance with statutory guidance and to ensure that the council’s housing policies benefit local people, applicants must have been continuously resident in Norwich for at least the last two years. If applicants cannot provide satisfactory evidence that they meet the criteria, an application will not be taken. For household members to join an application and to be included in any assessment of housing need, the same criteria apply. 2.5.4. Exceptional circumstances will be considered. In such cases, the decision as to whether an applicant qualifies will be determined by a Housing Options team leader or manager, or by the council’s assessment panel. 2.5.5. Examples are: • Somebody who needs to live in Norwich as they have a significant need to be near specific medical care which is unavailable elsewhere. • Applicants over 60 who have a specific need for sheltered housing in Norwich to be near medical care or family support unavailable elsewhere. • The applicant needs to move to Norwich where failure to meet that need would cause extreme hardship to themselves or others • Tenants of social housing needing to move to Norwich for work-related reasons where failure to meet that need would cause hardship, who can evidence that they meet the criteria set out in the 2015 Regulations (SI 2015/967). • Households accepted as homeless under the Housing Act 1996 where the council has accepted a fully duty to rehouse • Care leavers – Applicants aged 18-21 years (or up to 25 years old if they are pursuing a programme of education agreed in their pathway plan), who are owed a duty under Children Act 1989, section 23C • Applicants fleeing domestic abuse who are living in refuge accommodation or who need to move urgently for the safety and security of themselves and any dependent children. • Applicants that can demonstrate a lifelong residential connection to Norwich which has been broken for only a short time. • In the examples above, a ‘reduced preference’ will be applied to the applicant’s banding to ensure priority to long-term local residents. These are examples and this list is not exhaustive. 2.5.6. Residents in prison, bail hostel, hospital or approved premises, or those households referred into or placed into any form of accommodation in Norwich by another agency or local authority will not gain a local connection and time spent in such premises will not count toward local connection. 2.5.7. Applicants whose only residential connection to Norwich is through further education or student accommodation will not be considered as having gained local connection. Student accommodation is that provided by an educational establishment or where a student exemption certificate has been provided for council tax purposes. 2.5.8. Where an applicant has only become eligible for housing assistance in the last two years, their local connection will commence from the date they became eligible. 2.5.9. Where an application is taken from a client who has not lived in Norwich continuously for the previous two years, and the client would normally be placed in a priority band, a ‘reduced preference’ will apply until the two year connection is established. 2.6. Exception to the criteria: Armed and Reserve Forces 2.6.1. The council is committed to ensuring that service personnel and their families have access to appropriate accommodation when they leave the British armed forces. Under the terms of the Armed Forces Covenant, to which the council is signatory, the local connection criteria will not apply to the following: Those who are currently serving in the regular forces or who have served in the regular forces. • Bereaved spouses or civil partners of those serving in the armed and reserve forces where (i) the bereaved spouse or civil partner has recently ceased or will cease to be entitled to reside in Ministry of Defence accommodation following the death of their spouse or civil partner and (ii) the death was wholly or partly attributable to their service. • Existing or former members of the reserve forces who are suffering from a serious injury, illness or disability which is wholly or partly attributable to their service. • Divorced or separated spouses or civil partners of Service personnel who are required to move out of accommodation provided by the Ministry of Defence. Under these terms, the council can ensure that current and former service personnel in urgent housing need are awarded preference in line with the priority need bands. 2.7. Those who will not qualify: need considerations 2.7.1. Home Options policy aims to manage expectations realistically and to focus resources on those in most need of them. Therefore, having considered the provisions made in the Localism Act 2011, the following applicants will not qualify: • Applicants who are tenants of scheme landlords who have made a ‘right to buy’ application on their property. • Applicants who are tenants of scheme landlords and are in the process of carrying out a mutual exchange or have completed a mutual exchange in the previous 12 months. • Applicants who have been housed through the scheme will not be able to reapply for Home Options for a 12-month period from the commencement of their new tenancy. This restriction does not apply where the household circumstances have changed and the property is no longer suitable or where there are extenuating circumstances. • Applicants who have been housed through the council’s private sector leasing scheme (Let NCC) or through a loan from the council’s homeless prevention fund will have their Home Options application cancelled and will not be able to reapply for a 12-month period from the commencement of their new tenancy. This restriction does not apply where the household circumstances have changed and the property is no longer suitable or where there are extenuating circumstances. • Clients who have been sponsored to enter the country in the last five years based on an undertaking given by a sponsor that accommodation was available (and where that sponsor is still alive) • Applicants who own or have an interest in a property as a freeholder, leaseholder, a part-owner through shared ownership, including part commercial/residential property, in the UK or abroad will not qualify unless there are extenuating circumstances, as determined by a review panel. Examples of extenuating circumstances could be someone who requires sheltered housing in Norwich or someone who has been accepted as statutorily homeless. 2.8. Those who will not qualify: behaviour considerations 2.8.1. The council, scheme landlords and Norwich residents have a right to expect certain standards of behaviour. Where an applicant or a member of their household has a history of behaviour which is evidenced to have caused a detrimental effect to others, the Council may decide that the applicant does not qualify to be accepted onto the Home Options scheme. 2.8.2. Some examples of the type of behaviour that could mean that an applicant does not qualify for the Home Options scheme are: • Serious rent arrears which, in the council’s view, would entitle the landlord to a possession order. • Causing deliberate damage to a property. • Causing anti-social behaviour such as nuisance to neighbours, discriminatory behaviour or harassment, abuse, violence, or intimidation to the community or to council staff. • Conviction for using or allowing a property to be used for illegal or immoral purposes • Committing domestic abuse. • Conviction for violent crime or the supply, use or possession of drugs. • Conviction of a criminal offence in the property or in the locality of the property • Eviction from hostel or temporary accommodation • Being convicted of, issued with, or accepted a sanction for Benefit or Council Tax fraud within the last five years. • Making a false statement in order to obtain accommodation • Failing to provide relevant information that has been reasonably requested to verify an application for housing • Failing to allow contractors to enter the property to carry out maintenance. • Requesting or colluding with a landlord or family member to issue them with a Notice to Quit. These are examples and this list is not exhaustive 2.8.3. The examples relate to both current and former tenancies and apply no matter who the landlord is, when they happened or what form of tenancy was held. Paragraphs 15.3 & 15.4, together with Appendix B, deal with the way in which applicants may demonstrate that they have addressed past behaviour in order to requalify. 2.8.4. Decisions are made on a case-by-case basis, with each case judged on its own merits. 2.9. Public protection arrangements 2.9.1. Applicants subject to multi-agency public protection arrangements can only access the register with the consent of the Housing Options manager. Each case will be considered on its own merits in determining whether an application will be accepted. 2.10. Assessment of applications 2.11. Legal background 2.11.1. All applicants who are eligible and who qualify for Home Options will be placed in the appropriate banding based on an assessment of their housing needs. This is to ensure that the council allocates homes to those in the greatest assessed need and to ensure that its legal obligations are met. 2.11.2. The council is required by law to give reasonable preference in the scheme to people with high levels of assessed housing need: • People who need to move on welfare or medical grounds (including grounds relating to a disability), • People who need to move to a particular locality of the city to avoid hardship to themselves or others, • People living in unsanitary, unsatisfactory, or overcrowded housing, and • People who are homeless within the meaning of the Housing Act 1996, and people who are owed a particular statutory duty by any local housing authority under section 190(2), 193(2) or 195(2) (or under section 65(2) or 68(2) of the Housing Act 1985 or who are occupying accommodation secured by any such authority under section 192(3). • Former and serving members of the armed or reserve forces who have an urgent housing need or need to move because of a serious injury, medical condition or disability sustained as a result of their service • Bereaved spouses and civil partners of members of the armed forces leaving services family accommodation following the death of their spouse or partner 2.11.3. Applicants outside the reasonable preference categories can also be given additional consideration to meet local priorities. 2.11.4. Applications are processed by the council’s Home Options team, in accordance with this policy. 3. The housing need bands 3.1. Each application will be assessed to determine the level of housing need of the household and placed into one of five bands: Emergency Band Emergency priority Gold Band High priority Silver Band Medium priority Bronze Band Emergency/high/medium priority but with reduced preference Standard Band No priority 3.2. Banding will only be awarded where the applicant’s circumstances have been verified. 3.3. An applicant’s circumstances and therefore their level of housing need and banding is subject to change. As such, an applicant’s Home Options banding is kept under continuous review. 3.4. Every applicant is responsible for ensuring that they provide correct and up to date information. 3.5. The criteria for being placed in each band are as follows: 3.6. Emergency band 3.6.1. This band is intended to meet the needs of applicants in extreme circumstances and will only be issued in certain situations where an applicant needs urgent re-housing to ensure their well-being or safety. An applicant in Emergency band is expected to place two bids per week with the guidance of their housing adviser and accept the first suitable available property which they successfully bid for. As examples, circumstances where emergency status may be awarded include: • An applicant has an extremely urgent medical need, as determined by a Housing Options team leader or manager or the council’s assessment panel. • Those applicants requiring urgent hospital discharge where their current accommodation is totally unsuitable for their needs • Those applicants required to leave their homes as a result of an emergency prohibition order served in relation to the premises under the Housing Act 2004 or as the result of action taken by the Norfolk Fire and Rescue Service • Other extreme circumstances as determined by the Housing Options manager or assessment panel. 3.7. Gold band 3.7.1. Homelessness and homeless prevention: Applicants to whom the council has accepted a prevention of homelessness duty, where their circumstances have been confirmed and who are assessed by their housing adviser as likely to be in priority need. Applicants will have completed and kept to a personalised housing plan made with a housing adviser, will place, or have placed for them, two bids per week with the guidance of their adviser and will be entitled to one suitable offer of accommodation. In such circumstances the need to prevent or relieve homelessness may supersede other housing considerations. Refusal of the offer or failure to engage with advice will mean the council’s duty is ended and gold banding will be removed. 3.7.2. Severe medical need: Critical medical needs directly relating to the applicant’s accommodation or need for accommodation as determined by a Housing Options team leader or manager, or by the council’s assessment panel. Medical priority is only awarded where, in the assessment of the panel, an applicant needs urgent re-housing due to a strongly evidenced, serious and enduring medical condition or disability, which is severely and permanently affected by their current accommodation. Examples of severe medical need determining the award of gold band: • The applicant is housebound through mobility issues and moving to alternative accommodation would alleviate this. • The applicant’s life is at risk. • The applicant is unable to move around their current accommodation, and cannot access kitchen or bathing facilities • A member the household is severely disabled and needs substantial adaptations to help meet their needs but these cannot be carried out in their current accommodation • The applicant has a terminal illness and alternative accommodation would allow for suitable care to be provided • The applicant has a severe and enduring medical condition which is significantly exacerbated by poor housing conditions and the accommodation cannot be repaired and no other remedies are available. • Armed Forces members and veterans suffering from mental or physical ill health as a result of their service. These are examples and this list is not exhaustive. 3.7.3. Welfare Where the applicant or member of their household assessed by the panel as being grievously and adversely affected by their current accommodation and there is an urgent need to move for welfare reasons. This may include situations such as: • Infirmity due to old age • The need to give or receive care • A vulnerable applicant is being exploited within their accommodation putting them at risk • To help avoid a residential placement where an applicant, with the necessary support mechanisms in place, is capable and best suited to independent living. • The applicant is participant is a witness protection programme This list is not exhaustive and other exceptional circumstances will be considered. Assessment will be subject to a thorough investigation of all the circumstances by the council’s assessment panel and the degree of priority awarded will depend on the circumstances of the case. 3.7.4. Housing Conditions Applicants have no access to a kitchen and/or bathroom. Or A prohibition order or demolition order has been served in relation to the applicant’s dwelling by the council’s private sector housing team. This indicates that the property contains one or more category 1 hazards that probably cannot be remedied. Or An improvement notice has been served in relation to the applicant’s dwelling by the private sector housing team and: • The remedies that are needed to reduce the hazard will require the property to be vacated for a significant period • The cost of the remedies is beyond the means of the applicant (where applicable) • The remedies will make the property unsuitable for occupation by the applicant In such cases the award of priority banding is dependent upon individual circumstances, which will be considered on a case-by-case basis by a Housing Options team leader or manager. 3.7.5. Overcrowding Applicants lack two or more bedrooms. 3.7.6.
