Under-occupation/council interest Tenants of council or scheme landlord accommodation that are under occupying by two or more bedrooms and prepared to move to significantly smaller accommodation or are occupying a substantially adapted property that they no longer require that the housing options manager assesses would be in high demand from applicants in need of those adaptations. 3.7.7. Decommissioning Where a cabinet decision has been made to decommission a council property, gold band will be awarded to any tenant having to move home as a result. 3.7.8. Violence/Harassment Where there is significant evidence of serious ongoing harassment or violence toward a household, where a change of accommodation within Norwich could be reasonably expected to alleviate the problem and there is no other remedy. In such instances banding will be awarded by a housing advisor working with the client to prevent their homelessness or as the result of a of a submission to the assessment panel. 3.7.9. Care leavers Where an applicant is leaving local authority care and is assessed as needing to move on (as determined by a Housing Options team leader or manager following the required evidence and risk assessment being submitted from Children’s Services), where the applicant has completed a tenancy awareness course, support plan outcomes have been met and there is a suitable support package in place so that the council is satisfied that the applicant is able to successfully manage their own tenancy. Referrals can be accepted from four weeks before the applicant leaves care. Applicants will have completed and kept to a personalised housing plan made with a housing adviser, will place two bids per week with the guidance of their adviser and will be entitled to one suitable offer of accommodation. Refusal of the offer will mean that gold banding will be removed. 3.7.10. Let NCC Where the applicant meets the criteria set out under the LetNCC tenant incentive scheme (Appendix C) 3.7.11. Multiple Needs Applicants with a combination of medium needs. 3.8. Silver band 3.8.1. Homelessness and homeless prevention Applicants to whom the council has accepted a prevention of homelessness or relief of homelessness duty, where their circumstances have been confirmed and who are assessed by the council’s housing advice team as not likely to be in priority need. Applicants will have completed and kept to a personalised housing plan made with a housing adviser, will place or have placed for them two bids per week with the guidance of their adviser and will be entitled to one offer of accommodation. In such circumstances the need to prevent or relieve homelessness may supersede other housing considerations. Refusal of the offer or failure to engage with advice will mean the council’s duty is ended and silver banding will be removed. 3.8.2. Medical Significant medical needs directly relating to the applicant’s accommodation or need for accommodation as determined by a Housing Options team leader, manager or by the council’s assessment panel. For example: • Applicants with an evidenced, enduring, and significant medical or disability problem which seriously affects their ability to manage in their current accommodation, where a move would resolve the issue and no other remedy is available. 3.8.3. Welfare Where, in the assessment of the panel, the applicant or member of their household is evidenced as being seriously and adversely affected by their current accommodation, the issue cannot be remedied and there is a significant need to move for welfare reasons. Assessment will be subject to a thorough investigation of all the circumstances and the degree of priority awarded by the council’s assessment panel will depend on the circumstances of the case. 3.8.4. Housing Conditions A hazard awareness notice has been served by the council’s private sector housing team. In relation to a category 1 or 2 hazard at the applicant’s dwelling and: • The remedies that are needed to reduce the hazard will require the property to be vacated for a significant period; or • The cost of the remedies is beyond the means of the applicant (where applicable); or • The remedies will make the property unsuitable for occupation by the applicant • A suspended improvement notice or prohibition order exists but a foreseeable change in the applicant’s circumstances will cause it to become active and result in a high priority situation. In such cases the award of priority banding is dependent upon individual circumstances, which will be considered on a case-by-case basis. 3.8.5. Overcrowding Applicants lack one bedroom and those verified as ‘sofa surfing’. 3.8.6. Under-occupation Applicants in general stock council or scheme landlord accommodation, who are under occupying by one bedroom and are willing to move to smaller accommodation. 3.8.7. Children in flats or maisonettes 3.8.7.1 Applicants with a child or children aged ten or under and living in a flat or maisonette that does not have its own garden or private outdoor space. 3.8.7.2 Where a household includes a child or children aged six or under and the applicant lives in a property on the third floor or above where there is no lift access, an extra unit of priority will be added. Please note that any combination of issues related to children in flats would not normally exceed gold band. 3.8.7.3 This category will not be awarded for those children who were born when the current accommodation was accepted. 3.8.8. Let NCC Where the applicant meets the criteria set out under the LetNCC tenant incentive scheme (Appendix C) 3.8.9. Rough sleeping This priority will be applied where it has been confirmed that an applicant is sleeping rough, meets the qualification criteria and it has been assessed that there is no other accommodation available to them. The council will carry out a needs-led assessment and use professional judgement to engage and support people sleeping rough in each case. Priority will not be awarded when the client does not engage with the council’s support or where accommodation has been made available to the applicant which they have chosen not to accept. Any banding determination will be made in conjunction with the council’s rough sleeping team. Applicants assessed as ‘sleeping rough’ will not be awarded additional priority on any other accommodation related factors. 3.9. Bronze band (reduced preference) 3.9.1. Reduced preference Applicants with one of the assessed needs as detailed in emergency, gold, or silver band but who have been assessed for reduced preference as set out in section 4.1. In such cases, any criteria applied to the original banding will apply equally once reduced preference has been applied. 3.10. Standard band All other applicants to the scheme will be placed in the standard band: 3.10.1. Adequately housed Applicants who live in a property that is adequate to meet their needs in terms of property type, size, and facilities. 3.10.2. Supported Housing/Hostels Applicants in supported housing/hostels and undergoing a resettlement programme and either not yet ready to move on or not engaging fully with the programme (based on the required evidence from an accredited supporting agency) Or Applicants in supported housing/hostels who do not participate in the hostel move on agreement. 3.10.3. Deliberate worsening of circumstances and becoming homeless intentionally Applicants who are assessed by the council as having created or worsened their housing circumstances through their own actions or omissions, including those found to be intentionally homeless under homelessness legislation. This includes applicants who would otherwise be in a priority band. Examples: • An applicant giving up accommodation that was suitable or more suitable for them than the accommodation they have moved into and which it was reasonable to continue to occupy. • An applicant creating overcrowding by allowing family and/or friends to move into their home, which has worsened their housing situation. • An applicant moving into a property that was unsuitable for their household needs from the outset. • An applicant being unable to continue to occupy accommodation due to their deliberate action or omission. • Homeowners who have transferred or gifted their property to another person • Applicants who have dispersed or deprived themselves of assets or capital which could have reasonably been used to secure housing. • Unreasonably failing to follow advice given by the council in order to prevent homelessness. These are examples and this list is not exhaustive There is no time limit on the imposition of standard band on these grounds. 4. Methods of assessment 4.1. Reduced preference 4.1.1. Section 166A(5) of the Housing Act 1996, as amended by the Homelessness Act 2002, allows allocation schemes to give reduced preference where the behaviour of an applicant (or member of their household) affects their suitability to be a tenant. 4.1.2. In such circumstances, where tenancy conditions have been breached, an assessment will be made as to whether the applicant’s behaviour merits their not qualifying for Home Options or whether an application can be taken and reduced preference applied. 4.1.3. An applicant will be given reduced preference if the council is satisfied they or a household member owes housing related debts or who has failed to maintain a rented property in a proper and reasonable condition. 4.1.4. Housing related debt includes but is not limited to: • Any current or former tenant rent arrears or charges for use and occupation owed to any local authority, registered provider or private sector landlord. • Unpaid sundry debts owing to any local authority, registered provider or private sector landlord, including rechargeable debts or court costs. • Any tenancy deposit or rent in advance loans provided by the council that remain unpaid; or tenancy deposit guarantees that have been honoured by the council and remain unpaid. • Outstanding council tax debts. • Outstanding re-chargeable repairs. • Current and former housing related service charge arrears. • Temporary accommodation charge arrears where that temporary accommodation was provided by the council. • Any court costs incurred by the council or a housing association associated with any of the above debts 4.1.5. In exceptional circumstances, applicants will be given additional preference despite meeting one of the criteria outlined above. Examples of where this may be appropriate are: • Where a scheme landlord seeks discretion as current rent arrears are caused by welfare reform due to under-occupation and the applicant is seeking to downsize, is keeping to a repayment arrangement and is working with the landlord to address arrears. • Where a person is fleeing violence or domestic abuse and has rent arrears. 4.2. Significant financial resources: 4.2.1. Applicants that have sufficient income or savings which it would be reasonable for them to use to meet their housing need through other tenures whose circumstances determine that they would otherwise be in emergency, gold or silver band will have their priority downgraded to bronze band. 4.2.2. This assessment will be based on the following: • The total income of the applicant/household • Any capital available to the applicant/household • Average property prices and rents in the area for the type of accommodation needed by the household • The ability of the applicant/partner to rent a property in the private sector based on a realistic assessment of their financial position and commitments. • The ability of the applicant/partner to acquire a mortgage and maintain required repayments based on a realistic assessment of their financial position and commitments. 4.2.3. Excluded from the above financial assessment will be any member of the Armed Forces who may have received a lump sum as compensation for an injury or disability sustained on active service. 4.3. Assessment of overcrowding The council will use the following guidelines to assess the level of overcrowding: • Assessments are made on the basis that the household is optimising the bedrooms available. • Couples, married couples and civil partners are expected to share a bedroom/bedspace. • A room intended as a bedroom but used for another purpose will still be classified as a bedroom. • Where a child has a home elsewhere but chooses to live with another adult, this will not be counted when assessing overcrowding. • A single person or couple can occupy one bedroom. • Two children of the same gender are expected to share a bedroom up to the age of 16. When the oldest child is 16 years old, the family is classed as lacking one bedroom. • Two children of different gender are expected to share a bedroom until the oldest child is 10 years old, at which time the family is classed as lacking one bedroom. • Where adults aged 16 or over are sharing a room, but not living as a couple, they will be classed as lacking one bedroom. • An infant under 6 months can share a bedroom with their parents. 4.4. Assessment of multiple/cumulative need Where a household’s circumstances meet more than one assessed housing need, this will be considered by the council when prioritising the applicant. When a household has two or more housing needs within any one band, they will be moved one band higher to take into account the multiple needs. Any assessment of cumulative need will not normally exceed gold band. 4.5. Assessment of medical needs 4.5.1. Priority will be awarded based on information supplied by the applicant 4.5.2. The role of the assessment panel is to assess the degree of medical need relating to an applicant’s current accommodation and whether this merits additional priority to move to a more suitable property. 4.5.3. A panel of team leaders and managers will assess each case on its merits to determine whether medical priority should be awarded. In complex cases the panel will include medical professionals. 4.5.4. Where an applicant’s ill health is not directly related to their present housing, then medical priority will not be awarded. 4.5.5. Disabled applicants with specific accessibility needs receive priority over other applicants when bidding for adapted properties. Where the medical panel has assessed that an applicant or household member has a specific medical need for adaptations which are not and cannot be provided at their current home, their Home Options application will be given an accessibility rating, which gives additional preference over applicants who are not in need of adaptations when bidding for adapted properties. 4.5.6. Where adaptations to the applicant’s home have been completed in the last 5 years in order to address a household medical need, no Home Options medical assessment will be considered unless there has been a significant change of circumstances. 4.5.7. Each household is restricted to submitting one Home Options medical assessment per annum unless there has been a significant change in circumstances such as a new diagnosis or significant deterioration in condition. 4.6. Assessment of welfare needs 4.6.1. This will be carried out by an assessment panel made up of Housing Options team leaders and/or managers. 4.6.2. Each case will be assessed on its merits to determine whether welfare priority should be awarded. The assessment panel will look at whether the situation is targeted, serious and enduring, whether it is directly affected by the applicant’s present housing and whether it would improve if the applicant were re-housed. 4.6.3. In some instances, the assessment panel may award priority banding on a time limited basis and/or apply conditions to bidding. 4.7. Assessment of under-occupation Priority for under-occupation will not be awarded where the applicant chose to move into a property which they would under-occupy and their circumstances have not changed. 4.8. Assessment of housing conditions This will be carried out by the council’s private sector housing team. Assessment will be carried out in line with the Housing, Health and Safety Rating System and priority awarded as set out in the bands above. 4.9. Assessment of homelessness This will be carried out by the council’s housing advice and homelessness service in line with the Housing Act 1996 as amended by the Homelessness Act 2002 and Homelessness Reduction Act 2018. Priority will be awarded as set out in the bands above. 4.10. Supported Housing/Hostels Applicants in supported living or hostels participating in the hostel move-on scheme will be allocated properties in accordance with that scheme (Appendix A) 4.11. Assessments for applicants who are members of staff or elected members of the council 4.11.1. Applications from elected members or members of their family will be dealt with by the Housing Options manager. The award of a priority band and/or an allocation to elected members or to members of their family will need to be authorised by the Chief Executive Officer. 4.11.2. Applications from staff members will be dealt with by the Housing Options manager. The award of a priority banding and /or an allocation to staff members will need to be authorised by the council’s Director with responsibility for housing. 4.12. Determination of application date All applications will be awarded an ‘effective date’ by the council. This is usually the date on which the Home Options application was made. The date will determine who is successful in being offered a property where two or more people from the same band bid on the same property. 4.13. Change in circumstances 4.13.1. If an applicant’s circumstances change it is their responsibility to inform the council so that their application can be reassessed. Examples of a change of circumstances could include the serious deterioration in a medical condition, threat of homelessness or an increase in household size due to the birth of a child. Following the reassessment, if the applicant moves into a higher band their effective date will be the date that the council was notified of, or provided with evidence of, their change of circumstances. Alternatively, if an applicant moves into a lower band then the effective date will revert to the original date they applied for Home Options. 4.13.2. It is the applicant’s responsibility to ensure that their contact details are kept up to date. 4.14. Revision of applications Every Home Options applicant is sent a revision form on the anniversary of their application to ensure that their circumstances are kept up to date. They are required to update, sign and return the form to confirm they wish to remain on the housing register. The Home Options application will automatically be cancelled if the form is not returned. 4.15. Property size qualification Each applicant will be assessed by the council, to determine what size of property they qualify for. It is expected that participating landlords will seek to maximise occupation of available properties. A general guide showing property size qualification for different household sizes is set out in a table at Appendix E however, each participating landlord may choose to take account of local issues in determining what household size is eligible to bid for a property. This will be made clear at point of advertisement. Any potential affordability or housing benefit issues arising from this will be discussed with the applicant prior to their accepting the tenancy. 4.16. Notification of applications Once a Home Options application has been assessed the applicant will receive notification from the council confirming the band in which they have been placed. 4.17. Cancellation of applications 4.17.1. Applications will be cancelled by the council for the following reasons: • The applicant requests cancellation • The applicant's circumstances change and they are no longer eligible • The applicant's circumstances change and they no longer qualify • The applicant fails to return a revision form • The applicant is found to have made a false or deliberately misleading statement in connection with their application • The applicant moves outside the Norwich boundary. • The applicant has refused offers or failed to attend viewings on three occasions, where no other restrictions apply. 4.18. Refusals or failure to attend viewings 4.18.1. Where no other restrictions apply to the award of banding and an applicant has bid for three properties, which they have refused or where they have failed to attend the viewing without good cause, then their circumstances and banding will be reviewed. If these refusals are considered by a Housing Options team leader or manager to be unreasonable or without grounds, then the Home Options application will be cancelled and no new application will be accepted for a minimum twelve-month period. 4.19. Misrepresentation or withholding of information 4.19.1. It is a criminal offence for anyone to try and obtain accommodation from the council by knowingly giving a false statement or withholding information. 4.19.2. If we suspect that an applicant has given false information or withheld information, we will investigate. The Home Options application will be suspended while the investigation is carried out. 4.19.3. Failure by an applicant, or someone acting at their instigation, to inform the council of changes to their application, contrivance of circumstances or the deliberate withholding, or misrepresentation of information relevant to their housing circumstances, will mean that the applicant will not to qualify for Home Options and their application will be cancelled for an indefinite period and can be reviewed only after a minimum twelve- month period. Any such action may also result in criminal prosecution. If found guilty the applicant could be liable to a fine and/or imprisonment. 4.19.4. The scheme landlord may seek possession of a tenancy that was granted as a result of a false statement and may also attempt to recover any costs incurred. 5. Accessing the housing options 5.1. Finding a home Once applicants are registered on Home Options they can start looking for a social housing property of their choice. 5.2. Advertising of vacant properties 5.2.1. Properties will be advertised on a weekly basis. 5.2.2. Properties will be advertised in two main categories. These will be: • For all applicants. • For existing (transfer) tenants of the council and scheme landlords only. • By these means the council will seek to ensure that at least 20% of allocations made through Home Options are to existing tenants. 5.2.3. Properties will be advertised in the following ways: • In a newsletter • At the council’s website 5.2.4. The Home Options bidding cycle runs for the seven days from Wednesday midnight each week. 5.3. Promotion of other housing options 5.3.1. Information will also be provided about the other housing options we will be promoting through the scheme including: • Help to stay in your current home (Disabled Facilities Grants, dementia grants and other discretionary loans etc.) • Rent Deposit Schemes • LetNCC scheme • Discretionary Housing Payments • Mutual exchanges • Help to access properties for shared ownership 5.4. Property descriptions 5.4.1. Properties advertised will, wherever possible, carry a photograph of the property or similar and will have a description of the property. This description will usually include the following information, provided by the landlord: • The type of property (house, flat etc.) • The tenure of the property (social rented housing, affordable rent, shared ownership etc.) • The number of bedrooms the property has • The location of the property • The level of accessibility the property has for people with mobility problems/wheelchair users • Any services provided to the property e.g. wardens, caretaker etc. • The heating type the property has • Any age restrictions on the property (sheltered etc.) • Whether pets are allowed • Availability of outside space (garden etc.) • The rent of the property and the service charges. Social rented properties can sometimes have two different rent levels of ‘social rent’ and ‘affordable rent’ and each landlord has their own criteria for which rent level applies to which type of property. This should be clearly explained on each advert, where this is relevant. • Special information (location of bus routes/ other amenities etc.) • Whether the property is available to all applicants or transfer applicants only 5.4.2. Applicants must qualify for the size of property as advertised. 5.4.3. The landlord will ascribe tenancy type(s) for their advertised properties. 5.5. Bidding/application process Provided the applicant meets the stated qualifying criteria they can bid for the property by the deadline given. 5.6. Deadlines for bids Bidding closes at midnight every Wednesday. Bids received after the specified deadline will not be considered unless there are extenuating circumstances. Any such retrospective bids must be agreed by the Housing Options manager and a record kept of the reasons for acceptance of the retrospective bid held on record for audit purposes. 5.7. Bidding methods Applicants can bid in the following ways: • On the website, www.norwichhomeoptions.org.uk • Over the telephone to the Home Options team. 5.8. Disqualified bids 5.8.1. Applicants are restricted to making two bids for social rented properties per week. Applicants will not be considered for any property for which they do not meet the qualifying criteria. For example, a single person would not be considered for a three-bedroom property. 5.8.2. Where an applicant who has been awarded a priority banding to reflect a specific housing need has bid for a property which does not meet this housing need, their bid will not be considered. For example, an applicant in a priority band based on a medical need for a ground floor property will not be considered if they have bid for a house or upper floor flat. 5.9. Selection of the successful bids 5.9.1. At the end of the advertising cycle a shortlist will be drawn up from all applicants that have applied for a property. At this point the banding and qualification of any shortlisted applicant will be reviewed for accuracy. 5.9.2. The offer of accommodation will be made to the person in the highest band that meets the qualifying criteria. If there is more than one applicant in the band, the offer will be made to any UK armed forces veteran within that band, followed by the applicant who has been waiting the longest within that band. If the applicant with the highest priority refuses the property it will be offered to the next highest bidder and so on. 5.9.3. In order to maximise use of adapted properties, where a property has had adaptations to improve accessibility, the scheme landlord has the right to allocate the property to the applicant that has bid who is in greatest need of those specific adaptations at that property. As such, an occupational therapist may be invited to viewings of adapted properties to advise on suitability. 5.9.4. A risk and support needs assessment may be carried out. As a result, restrictions may be placed on the area or property which the applicant will be considered for. Applicants will not be offered a property where a risk to themselves or others has been identified. 5.10. Making the offer 5.10.1. The successful applicant will be contacted by the landlord whose property they have applied for to arrange an accompanied viewing. More than one applicant may be invited to the viewing. Photographic identification from the applicant will be required at the viewing. 5.10.2. Applicants will usually be contacted within three working days of the advert for the property closing. If an applicant cannot be contacted following multiple attempts the next person on the shortlist will be contacted. It is therefore important that all applicants ensure they are contactable or else they may lose out on a property they have applied for. 5.10.3. Applicants have 48 hours to decide whether to accept the offer of accommodation. If no response has been received after this time, the next person on the shortlist will be offered the property. 5.10.4. If an applicant refuses the offer, the property will be offered to the next on the shortlist, and so on until the property is let. 5.10.5. Scheme landlords reserve the right to carry out an assessment on applicants to ensure the particular property is appropriate. If the landlord deems the property not to be suitable for the applicant, the property would then be offered to the next applicant on the shortlist. 5.10.6. Offers of accommodation may be withdrawn if it is found that the information supplied by the applicant was incorrect or if they are deemed due to their behaviour to not qualify (e.g. if they have accrued rent arrears that were not previously known about). 5.11. Hostel move-on The Norwich hostel move on agreement (appendix D) sets out how applicants in participant hostels and supported accommodation who meet the criteria will be allocated social housing. 5.12. Properties excluded from the scheme The council reserves the right to exclude certain properties and housing schemes from the allocations system. Examples of where this may occur are: • Where a property is needed urgently to deal with an emergency. • Specialist housing schemes, for example Housing with Care Schemes will also be let outside the allocations scheme. 5.13. Direct lets 5.13.1. In certain circumstances the council will allocate properties directly to applicants, outside of the usual process. 5.13.2. Illustrative examples of direct lets are as follows: • Where an allocation is required to ensure protection of the public, for example, following a decision made by a Multi-Agency Public Protection Panel meeting, or where an applicant has been referred as part of the witness protection scheme. • Where the council or a scheme landlord has entered a special arrangement with a support agency in order to accommodate especially vulnerable or challenging clients. Any such arrangement will be governed by an agreement signed off by the Head of Housing. • Where the tenant of a scheme landlord’s home is being repaired and is not occupiable so that they need to be moved from the property on a temporary or permanent basis. • Where a client has been accepted as statutorily homeless, they will be direct let the first suitable available property. • As part of the council’s ‘hostel move-on’ scheme (see Appendix D) 5.13.3. A tenancy may also be allocated by the council or scheme landlord, regardless of other priorities, where the applicant has enjoyed established occupancy of the property, has a reasonable expectation of a property of that type and would be a suitable tenant, (e.g. non-secure tenants, or carers or family members with no succession rights.) In deciding whether to make an offer of a tenancy the landlord will consider whether the property is of a suitable size and type for the applicant’s household and the conduct of the applicant in terms of rent arrears and tenancy conditions. 5.13.4. Decisions to allocate properties outside of Home Options will be authorised by the Housing Options manager and held on record. 5.14. Sensitive lets 5.14.1. Sensitive lets are used where a specific issue has been identified in a particular area or block, making a property unsuitable for allocation to some applicants. When considering a sensitive let, instead of allocating a property to the applicant at the top of the list, the landlord will consider the suitability of each applicant who has bid for the vacancy. This will be based on information held about the applicant and on knowledge of the property, its location or neighbours. 5.14.2. The council will only use sensitive lets in exceptional circumstances. In order to ensure that all decisions on sensitive lets are accountable, transparent and monitored, all decisions must be agreed by the Housing Options manager and the respective manager of the scheme landlord and a record held on file. 5.15. Local lettings plans 5.15.1. Local lettings plans are used by landlords to develop policies and letting arrangements that: • Respond to local housing need and demand • Help to suitably match applicants to properties; and • Help them to achieve a balanced housing mix within a particular area. The main aim of a local lettings plan is to build a strong and sustainable community. 5.15.2. Local lettings plans are generally used when allocating new build housing for the first time. New build developments are unusual in terms of housing allocations because of the number of properties that are available for let in a short period of time in one area. 5.15.3. This makes sure that: • new build programmes meet the widest possible range of needs; and • the council avoids the creation of groups of vulnerable households in specific communities. 5.15.4. To make sure that all decisions on local lettings agreements are accountable, transparent and monitored, all decisions must be agreed by the Housing Options manager and the respective manager of the scheme landlord and a record held on file. 5.16. Sheltered Housing 5.16.1. Sheltered housing is accommodation designed specifically for older people. Residents may pay an additional charge for support services. 5.16.2. The minimum age for the landlord to consider an applicant for sheltered housing will be clearly stated when each property is advertised. 5.16.3. The council and scheme landlords may carry out a needs and risk assessment for customers who bid for sheltered housing properties, to ensure the services provided are appropriate to their needs. This will be done as part of the offer process. 6. Statement on equal access 6.1.1. The council and scheme landlords are committed to ensuring equality of opportunity in all elements of the scheme. This means that we seek to ensure that priority for housing is based on housing need and that housing policies are fair to all sections of the community regardless of age, disability, gender, marriage and civil partnership, pregnancy and maternity, race, religion or belief, or sexual orientation. 6.1.2. We want our services to be accessible to everyone who lives in Norwich. If you need extra help to be able to use our services, such as translation and interpretation services, large print or signing, please tell us. 6.1.3. All applicants for housing or rehousing may be asked to provide details of age, disability, gender, marriage and civil partnership, pregnancy and maternity, race, religion or belief, or sexual orientation. This is to allow us to assess the application properly as well as to monitor who is allocated housing, and to ensure that properties are being offered and allocated fairly. 6.2. Advice and assistance The council will ensure that everybody in Norwich seeking housing can easily access the information and assistance they require to use the scheme effectively and we will provide advice on the range of housing options open to them. Staff will be available throughout office hours to provide advice and assistance on the full range of housing options available. 6.3. Vulnerable groups 6.3.1. Due to the nature of Home Options, particularly the need for applicants to be proactive in the process, the council realises it is essential that vulnerable and excluded people can participate effectively. The council will therefore ensure all relevant staff are well trained so that they can assist vulnerable applicants to access and use the scheme. 6.3.2. All literature will be available in a large font and written in plain and unambiguous language. The website is compatible with screen readers and has browse aloud capability. 6.3.3. The council will also hold an ‘assisted applicants list’ for those who, due to their vulnerability, require additional help with the scheme. This additional help includes helping applicants bid for available homes or sending the property brochures directly to people who cannot access the internet. 6.3.4. The ‘assisted applicants list’ can be accessed by applicants or their support workers informing the council. This service will only be available for the most vulnerable clients as determined by the council. 6.3.5. To ensure vulnerable groups are not being disadvantaged under the scheme, the council will monitor systems to ensure all groups are using the scheme successfully. 7. Reviews of decisions 7.1. Notifying an ineligible or non-qualifying applicant: 7.1.1. The council will notify an applicant in writing of any decision that they: • Are ineligible for Home Options • Do not qualify to join Home Options. In each instance, the council will give clear grounds for the decision. 7.1.2. An applicant can ask for a review of certain decisions made regarding Home Options. These are: • That they are not eligible or do not qualify • Their band and effective date • The type of property that they can bid/apply for 7.2. A request for a review of a decision must be made in writing within 21 days of receipt of the decision. The decision will be reviewed by an assessment panel made up of Housing Options team leaders and/or managers. The role of the reviewer is to ensure that policy has been correctly applied. We aim to complete all review and medical assessments within 56 days of the request but in some circumstances this timeframe may be extended. The applicant will be notified in writing of the decision. 7.3. In requesting a review of their qualification for Home Options, the applicant will normally be expected to show that they have addressed issues which caused them not to qualify for the scheme over a minimum 12-month period, clearly demonstrating to the council’s satisfaction that their behaviour has been addressed and they are able to independently maintain a tenancy. The applicant’s individual circumstances will be fully considered as part of any review and each case will be treated on its merits. 7.4. Where an applicant does not qualify for Home Options through rent arrears, the council has set out in Appendix B the repayment arrangements and timeframes expected to be maintained in order for the applicant to demonstrate that the issue is being satisfactorily addressed. 7.5. Once a review has been completed, an applicant does not have the right to ask for a further review on the same grounds. 7.6. Complaints procedure 7.6.1. If an applicant is dissatisfied with any aspect of the management of their Home Options application, other than where a review can be made, they should follow the council’s complaints procedure, details of which can be found at the website www.norwich.gov.uk. 7.6.2. The council will not accept a complaint for issues where there is or has already been a right of appeal, for example reviews of Home Options banding or qualification. 7.7. Local Government & Social Care Ombudsman If a complainant is not satisfied with the action the council takes, he or she can send a written complaint to the ombudsman. A complainant must give the organisation an opportunity to deal with a complaint first, using its complaints procedure. The Local Government & Social Care Ombudsman can be contacted at: Tel: 0300 061 0614. Website: www.lgo.org.uk 8. Confidentiality statement 8.1. Norwich City Council is committed to protecting the rights of privacy and processing will be conducted fairly, lawfully and transparently in accordance with the General Data Protection Regulation (EU 2016/679) and all other applicable data protection law (‘Data protection legislation’). 8.2. We will ensure the personal information of all applicants (new, existing and former) is: • Stored lawfully • Processed in a fair and transparent manner • Collected for a specific, explicit and legitimate purpose • The data will be kept up to date and held until it is no longer required • Shared only with other organisations for legitimate processing, the prevention of fraud or with the person’s explicit consent. Our Privacy Notice can be located online at: www.norwich.gov.uk 8.3. When an application is made to Home Options, the applicant will be asked to give permission for information to be obtained from, or shared with, third parties, which would be required to enable the Home Options assessment or an allocation of housing to proceed. 8.4. If an applicant bids on a property advertised on Home Options, their data will be shared with the council or housing association that owns the property to enable the accurate and fair matching of people to properties to take place. Home Options partners and housing associations may also make enquires with council housing benefit departments and other agencies such as medical practitioners, DWP, support agencies, police and landlords to confirm the details provided by applicants. 9. Monitoring/changes to the scheme 9.1. Scheme monitoring 9.1.1. The scheme will be monitored directly by the Housing Options manager. The manager will, where necessary make recommendations for changes to the scheme, taking into consideration the following: • Application and bidding data, property turnover and demand • That the highest needs applicants and those who are vulnerable are using the scheme effectively • The scheme’s performance in meeting its agreed aims • Feedback from applicants and stakeholders • That the scheme continues to address local housing issues. 9.2. Changes to the scheme The council reserves the right to expand, change or alter any element of the scheme, as and when required, to meet changes in housing need, capacity, resources and legislation. Any major changes to the scheme will be carried out through a report of the Housing Options Manager to the council executive, following consultation with scheme landlords. Appendix B - Equality Impact Assessment What is being assessed Norwich Home Options Allocation Policy Status Assessment of a statutory function update Officer completing this form Graduate Management Trainee Team Home Options Directorate Communities and Housing SLT sponsor Executive director of communities and housing Date assessment commenced 28th October 2025 Date of completion 4th November 2025 What are the main aims or purpose of the strategy, policy, plan, project, contract or major change to your service which you are considering? Part 4 of the Housing Act determines that local authorities must have an allocation scheme to determine priorities between applicants for Norwich City Council owned (social) housing and to set out the procedure to be followed when allocating social housing in their area. In Norwich, the allocation scheme is called Home Options. EQUALITY IMPACT ASSESSMENT Will the report this EqIA relates to go to Committee? Scrutiny Committee (15th January 2025) The current Home Options allocations policy dates from October 2021 and needs updating to incorporate new legislation and statutory guidance. The update also presents the opportunity to ensure that policy reflects local needs and issues. This EqIA covers the entire policy, highlighting specific proposed changes to the policy: (a) local connection requirement increased from 6 months to 2 years (b) reduction in permitted social housing refusals from 5 to 3 (c) prioritisation of armed forces veterans on housing shortlists within each band How does it fit with other services and policies, and how does it support our corporate priorities? Revisions to the Housing Allocations policy were developed in parallel with the development of the Norwich Homelessness and Rough Sleeping Strategy (2025–2030). These policy changes are closely aligned with the strategy and support the operational work of the homelessness prevention and relief teams. The revised housing register eligibility and prioritisation criteria will promote social housing allocation to the most vulnerable local people who are engaged with home options, including those at risk of homelessness or who are currently homeless. These policy revisions will influence both who can join the register and how quickly they may be allocated housing. The new housing allocation policy aligns to the “A Fairer Norwich” community-led plan priority: working to support local people and families so that they can face economic and social challenges. The policy aims to reduce inequality and the negative effects of poverty by prioritising social housing allocation for those who are the most in need within our city. What is the reason for the proposal or change (financial, legal etc)? The council has a statutory requirement to review and update their housing allocations policy in line with any significant changes to legislation, local priorities or local needs. In line with the update of the Homelessness and Rough Sleeping strategy (2025-2030), the allocations policy was reviewed and updated. Who will be affected by this strategy, policy, plan, project, contract or major change to your service? (Please tick all that apply) ☒ Residents ☐ Visitors ☐ Council Staff ☐ Businesses ☐ Workers Please state any specific client group or groups Specific groups impacted by this policy are: • Norwich City Council social housing tenants • Individuals applying for Norwich City Council home options • Individuals at risk of homelessness • Individuals experiencing homelessness Which wards will be impacted by your proposal? Does your proposal impact any of the council’s Reducing Inequality Target Areas (RITAs)? ☒ ALL Norwich City Council wards ☐ Bowthorpe ☐ Catton Grove ☐ Crome ☐ Eaton ☐ Lakenham ☐ Mancroft ☐ Mile Cross ☐ Nelson ☐ Sewell ☐ Thorpe Hamlet ☐ Town Close ☐ University ☐ Wensum ☒ Catton Grove ☒ North City Centre ☒ Earlham ☒ Pilling Park ☒ Heartsease ☒ Vauxhall Street ☒ Mid Lakenham ☒ West Pottergate and Russell Street ☒ Mile Cross What outcomes do you want to achieve, why and for who? Norwich has experienced significant population growth over the last decade and is the most densely populated district in Norfolk. Norwich, as with any city, faces some challenges including significant and entrenched inequality and deprivation: the latest data published by the End Child Poverty Coalition shows that between 2023-2024, 35.3% of children in Norwich were living in households below the poverty line. As of October 2025, Norwich City Council owns a total of 14,211 properties, which includes 13,291 general needs homes and 920 sheltered homes. Despite this stock, the 2021 Greater Norwich Housing Needs Assessment projected a significant shortfall in social housing provision. Demand continues to outpace supply, particularly among Home Options applicants who are unable to access the increasingly unaffordable private rental sector. The need for appropriate housing for vulnerable individuals and families is both urgent and well-evidenced. Homelessness is associated with significant health consequences for all experiencing it, including mental illness, infectious disease, heart disease, and early mortality (Crisis UK). Young people experiencing housing instability are more likely to be absent or excluded from school, while parents face heightened risks of depression and anxiety due to housing insecurity (Local Government Association, 2017). Older adults, particularly those over 60, are at increased risk of developing depression and dementia (Local Government Association, 2017). Temporary accommodation (TA) exacerbates these issues: two-thirds of TA residents report its negative impact on their mental and physical health (Shelter, 2023), and children residing in temporary housing for over a year are three times as likely to experience anxiety, depression, and infection compared to their housed peers (Shelter, 2006). Once within the social housing system, household changes can lead to overcrowding; a lack of available, larger homes prevents households from moving, thereby increasing their likelihood of mental illness, sleep disturbance, second-hand tobacco exposure, relationship breakdown, and poor educational attainment for children (WHO, 2018). A lack of stable housing additionally negatively impacts job and educational attainment, perpetuating the factors that entrap individuals in poverty and increase their need for social housing provision to prevent their homelessness (Crisis UK). Certain groups are disproportionately affected by homelessness risk or its negative consequences, including families with children, those who are pregnant, army veterans, care leavers, refugees, those fleeing abuse, those experiencing severe mental illness, and those with complex, multiple needs (St Martin in the Fields UK). To mitigate these harms and prevent homelessness among the most vulnerable through a very limited number of council-owned homes, the Home Options allocation policy must prioritise those in greatest need within Norwich. This prioritisation is primarily guided by statutory and legislative frameworks, supplemented by locally informed criteria that reflect emerging trends and community needs. What evidence and data has been used for this assessment, including community engagement and consultation? The new home options allocation policy will go through numerous stages of consultation and debate before sign-off. The draft policy revisions, alongside its summary report and this EqIA, will be uploaded to Get Talking Norwich for the public to view, to allow engagement and comments from the community. The results of this consultation will be considered before the revised policy is assessed and debated within scrutiny committee. This EqIA will also be revised following public consultation. Amendments and suggestions from scrutiny committee will be implemented as appropriate before the final revised policy will go to the council’s cabinet for sign off. Who implements, carries out or delivers the policy, practice, service or function? The home options, homelessness prevention, and homelessness relief teams. documents.title: Minutes of the Cabinet meeting held on 11 February 2026
documents.text: MINUTES Cabinet 17:38 to 19:15 Wednesday, 11 February 2026 Present: Councillors Stonard (Leader), Hampton (Deputy Leader and Cabinet Member for Climate and Environment), Giles (Cabinet Member for Planning and Regulatory Services), Harper (Cabinet Member for Finance and Major Projects), Jones (Cabinet Member for Housing), Kidman (Cabinet Member for Culture and Wellbeing) and Padda (Cabinet Member for Equalities and Social Justice). Apologies: None In attendance Councillor Galvin (Leader of the Green Group) 112. Adjournment 112.1 Due to a disruption the meeting was adjourned from 17:38 to 17:59 to allow for the room to be cleared. 113. Declarations of interest 113.1 Councillor Giles declared an other registerable interest in item 7: Motion 11B – Enhanced Paternity and Adoption Leave for Council – Referred by Council as he worked for UNISON but did not represent local government workers in Norfolk. 114. Public questions and petitions 114.1 There had been no public questions or petitions received. 115. Questions to cabinet members 115.1 The Leader announced that there had been one question received from Members of the Council to be put to Cabinet Members for which notice had been given in accordance with the provisions of Part 3 of the Council’s Constitution. 115.2 The question is summarised as follows: 115.3 Councillor Stutely to the Cabinet Member for Planning and Regulatory Services on the Norwich Airport Surface Access Strategy. Cabinet: 11 February 2026 115.4 Full details of the question and response were available on the Council’s website prior to the meeting. A revised version is attached to these minutes at Appendix A and includes a minute of any supplementary questions and responses. 116. Minutes 116.1 The minutes of the meeting held on 6 January 2026 were confirmed as a correct record. The minutes of the meeting held on 14 January 2026 would be taken to the next meeting. 117. Motion 11B – Enhanced Paternity and Adoption Leave for Council Employees – Referred by Council 117.1 The Cabinet Member for Equalities and Social Justice presented the item. She considered that the Scrutiny Committee should consider the motion and the options available to the Council, including communicating with the Trade Unions, before it returned to Cabinet. 117.2 Councillor Galvin asked the following question: “I hope that this motion can be taken forward by cabinet and not stalled further, as council had indicated its support and there are many staff and their families, not to mention newborn babies and mothers, who will benefit. Will you reassure me that you are putting their needs first?” 117.3 The Cabinet Member for Equalities and Social Justice gave the following response: “The UK is implementing major reforms in April 2026 under the Employment Rights Act 2025. These changes transform paternity and parental leave from "earned" rewards into immediate "day-one" rights law has finally made paternity leave a 'day- one' right for everyone. By enhancing our local offer, we are doing three things: Supporting Local Parents: Giving mums, dads and partners the real chance to bond and support their families without fearing the bills. Retaining Talent: We want to be the best employer in the area. Flexible, fair leave keeps our best staff from moving elsewhere. Fairness for All: It helps close the gender pay gap by making sure childcare isn't just 'women’s work'. We would like to reassure members that options set out before full council in January will be presented to Scrutiny Committee for further reflection and robustness, including engagement with relevant trade union bodies.” 117.4 The Cabinet Member for Equalities and Social Justice moved, and the Deputy Leader and Cabinet Member for Climate and Environment seconded that the item be referred to the Scrutiny Committee for its views before it was considered by Cabinet. Cabinet: 11 February 2026 117.5 RESOLVED to ask Scrutiny Committee to review the motion and that this is returned to Cabinet for a final decision. 118. The Council’s 2026-2027 Budget and Medium Term Financial Strategy 118.1 The Cabinet Member for Finance and Major Projects presented the report using slides (which are available on the Council’s website). The 2026-2027 financial year would be a year of major change and unlike previous financial years, the 2026- 2027 budget would be the final full budget before Local Government Reorganisation. There was a high level of complexity which included the uncertainty around costs, system alignment as the new models were designed, alongside the work transition and major one-off costs. Decisions around strategic priorities would need to be taken. Demand for the Council’s services continued to rise, with inflation remaining persistent. The budget looked at meeting current pressures against future priorities while protecting services. 118.2 The main budget areas for consideration were the general fund, Housing Revenue Account and capital expenditure. These were detailed in the agenda pack and the slides. She thanked the Scrutiny Committee for the work that it had conducted in scrutinising the budget and the budget setting process. The recommendations were noted and would be fed into future budget setting processes as appropriate. 118.3 She commended the budget to Cabinet that had been developed in the context of sustained financial pressure, ongoing demand for services and continued uncertainty around the costs of Local Government Reorganisation. The budget was balanced and responsible that protected core services, invested in the Council’s priorities and priorities that residents had highlighted. Financial resilience was a key part of the budget and the budget included a £1million contingency for Local Government Reorganisation. 118.4 The Council was proposing a 2.99% increase in the Council’s element of Council Tax. This was a proportionate increase that reflected the financial realities of the Council. A prudent minimum level of general fund reserves of £5.5million. She referred members to the section 25 assurance from the s151 Officer that the budget was robust, estimates were considered sound and that financial risk was appropriately managed. 118.5 The budget was supported by the Treasury Management Strategy to ensure that investments were managed prudently and sustainably. The budget aligned with the Council’s corporate priorities as detailed in the Council’s community-led plan “We are Norwich”. 118.6 The Cabinet Member for Housing seconded the report. She highlighted that the Housing Revenue Account (HRA) was a significant part of the budget and the proposed budget underlined the Council’s commitment in the housing stock and the challenges that the Council faced. As part of this the Council had considered the rent levels and were proposing an increase in rents of 4.8%. This enabled continued maintenance and improvement of the stock. A significant amount of work had already been done but more was planned which included a new capital works programme. Cabinet: 11 February 2026 118.7 Councillor Galvin asked the following question: “Scrutiny flagged that this is a relatively healthy budget with some headroom and the importance of making sure that this council continues to deliver through the turbulent times of Local Government Reorganisation and the huge changes ahead. The committee heard that a key issue is the costs coming our way, with at least £1m earmarked for the changes alone in this coming first year. Some councils in the same position are forecasting a £25m cost over three years. We clearly can’t afford this and need to keep track on this spending and its impacts. Will you commit to asking the government for extra support, especially if the changes start to impact the most vulnerable?” 118.8 The Cabinet Member for Equalities and Social Justice gave the following response: “The Council will continue to engage with the government through established channels on key funding matters. Local Government Reorganisation represents one of the most significant changes to public service delivery in a generation. It offers opportunities to improve operational efficiency, with any resulting savings contributing to the investment required throughout the post reorganisation payback period.” 118.9 The Cabinet Member for Finance and Major Projects moved, and the Cabinet Member for Housing seconded the recommendations for the reasons set out in the report. 118.10 RESOLVED to: 1) Note the latest financial information, the budget strategy incorporated into the report and the budget proposals, which enable the Council to set a balanced budget for 2026-2027 and Medium-Term Financial Strategy for the period to 2030-2031. 2) Note the Section 25 report of the chief finance officer on the robustness of the budget estimates, the adequacy of reserves, and the key financial risks to the Council 3) Note that the Council Tax resolution for 2026-2027 prepared in accordance with sections 32-36 of the Local Government Finance Act 1992 as amended by the Localism Act 2011, will be calculated and presented to Council for approval on 24 February 2026, once Norfolk County Council and the Office of the Police and Crime Commissioner for Norfolk have agreed the precepts for 2026-2027. 4) Recommend to Council to approve: General Fund i. The council’s net revenue budget requirement as £24,250,000 for the financial year 2026-2027 including the budget allocations to services shown in and the growth proposals set out in Section 2. Cabinet: 11 February 2026 ii. An increase to Norwich City Council’s element of the council tax of 2.99%, meaning that that the Band D council tax will be set at £315.26 (Section 2, paragraph 2.14) with the impact of the increase for all bands shown in Section 2, Appendix 2 (D). iii. The prudent minimum level of reserves for the council as £5,500,000 (Section 2, paragraph 2.29). iv. Delegation to the chief finance officer (S151 Officer) in consultation with the portfolio holder for Finance and Major Projects inclusion of any minor changes consequent on the final local government settlement or additional grant allocations. v.
