Corporate Performance Report 2025-2026 – Quarter Three 119.1 The Leader of the Council presented the report. The report covered 1 October to 31 December 2025. Overall performance remained steady with 68% of Key Performance Indicators (KPIs) were on or above target, 16% showed early warning signs, 16% had reached a level where intervention was required and 1 KPI was pending verification and would be reported in quarter four. 119.2 The areas requiring improvement included: • Rent collection – there had been a 2% rise in performance in quarter two but Universal Credit delays continued to drive arrears. A new workload system was being introduced to improve efficiency • Re-let times had increased to 51 days primarily due to a transition to a new fire safety door contractor, the issue had been resolved and was not expected to recur. • Temporary accommodation demand mirrored national trends requiring ongoing intensive management and careful use of targeted funding. 119.3 Performance improvements had been seen in the following areas: • Housing Benefit processing remained strong at 20.9 days to process new claims which met the 21-day target. • The delivery of the Warm Homes: Local Grant was progressing well with 50 private-sector energy efficiency measures installed in quarter three and further large-scale delivery planned through to 2028 Cabinet: 11 February 2026 • Customer satisfaction had increased following successful recruitment and digital channel use increased as more customers accessed services online. 119.4 A detailed overview of all performance data was available in the Corporate Performance Dashboard on the Council’s website. 119.5 Councillor Galvin asked the following question: “Average relet time of voids is persistently high due to some known factors, and we are not alone in this as an area. However, because improving this, even by a fraction a month, is something that can make so much difference and help us to house people, could the cabinet member outline exactly what she is doing to look at how we are improving the process by which we update stock and relet it, from key hand in, to new residents stepping over the mat?” 119.6 The Cabinet Member for Housing gave the following response: “Turnaround times for empty homes remain a persistent challenge, and this is an issue faced widely across the housing sector. Our current performance is broadly consistent with what we have seen in previous years. We fully recognise the impact that delays can have on residents waiting for a home, and improving void turnaround times continues to be a priority. We are actively focused on delivering further progress to ensure homes are returned to use as efficiently as possible To drive improvement, we have put in place a number of targeted and practical actions that strengthen the entire end‑to‑end process — from the moment keys are handed back, through works on the property, to letting the home to its new residents. These include: • Boosting capacity at the earliest stage, through the appointment of an additional voids surveyor. This is already helping us speed up initial inspections and get works progressing sooner. • Increasing our ability to manage major voids, by engaging two subcontractors to undertake larger and more complex jobs. This allows our in-house team to concentrate on minor works, improving throughput and reducing bottlenecks. • Mobilising two major capital contractors to help address long-standing investment needs across our stock. As these improvements progress, we expect to see fewer homes requiring extensive works at re-let, helping us bring properties back into use more quickly. • Reviewing the full voids and lettings process, strengthening hand-offs between teams, removing avoidable delays, and ensuring we are prioritising works in a way that maximises the flow of homes ready to let. In addition, our tenancy visit programme is helping us identify households who may need support to maintain their home. By intervening earlier, we can prevent properties falling into more significant disrepair, which in turn improves both the condition of our homes and future re-let performance. Cabinet: 11 February 2026 Even small improvements in turnaround times make a real difference to the number of families and individuals we can house each year. We are committed to sustaining the progress already made and continuing to reduce re-let times wherever possible.” 119.7 As Portfolio Holder the Cabinet Member for Housing monitored re-let times on a monthly basis, both formally through the housing performance dashboards and through briefings. Different areas were being explored including any small wins and what created different challenges at different times. Several properties that were handed back to the Council had been occupied for decades where upgrades had been declined at different times. More work was required to work with tenants to understand why upgrades were not taken. She was confident in the work that was being delivered. 119.8 The Leader of the Council moved, and the Deputy Leader and Cabinet Member for Climate and Environment seconded the recommendations for the reasons set out in the report. 119.9 RESOLVED that progress on key performance indicators for quarter three of 2025-2026 had been reviewed. 120. 2025-2026 Quarter Three Budget Monitoring Report 120.1 The Cabinet Member for Finance and Major Projects presented the report. The Cabinet was asked to note the forecast underspend in the General Fund. There was forecast underspends in both the General Fund and Housing Revenue Account capital programmes. Reasons for these underspends were detailed in the report. Cabinet were asked to approve the addition of £119,000 to the 2025-2026 Capital programme that was fully funded through external grants. 120.2 The Cabinet Member for Housing commented on the underspends in the HRA Capital programme. Capital works programme often did not run year-end to year- end. The Council was brining on board new contractors to conduct capital works over a longer term. 120.3 Councillor Galvin asked the following question: “Regarding resources, we are told there is a “necessity to fill some vacant posts with interim staff whilst a route to permanent recruitment is considered” on p182. What are the challenges Local Government Reorganisation poses to permanent recruitment and how are these challenges being mitigated?” 120.4 The Cabinet Member for Finance and Major Projects gave the following response: “The ongoing Local Government Reorganisation (LGR) programme requires the Council to exercise caution in making permanent appointments while the Government considers the proposals for establishing a new unitary authority. As noted in the LGR documentation, there is a recognised “necessity to fill some vacant posts with interim staff whilst a route to permanent recruitment is Cabinet: 11 February 2026 considered.” This reflects the uncertainty inherent in structural change across multiple authorities. Until the Government confirms the future governance arrangements, the organisational structure of a potential unitary authority remains unclear. This creates uncertainty about future service delivery models, staffing levels, and role profiles. Recruiting permanently into roles that may be redesigned, merged, or relocated carries significant risk both for the organisation and prospective candidates. The measures to mitigate these risks include: Filling essential posts with interim or agency staff to ensure continued service delivery while allowing flexibility to adjust once Government decisions are confirmed. This approach avoids long‑term financial commitments while protecting statutory and operational functions. Offering fixed‑term contracts aligned to LGR milestones can attract a broader applicant pool than interim roles. It provides clarity to candidates while preserving organisational flexibility until future structures are agreed. Providing transparent information about the LGR timeline, potential structural changes and reassurances regarding organisational commitment to supporting staff, helps mitigate concerns and maintain confidence. Implementing internal support measures such as wellbeing interventions, career conversations, and temporary role enhancements can help retain current staff during the period of uncertainty. Close co-ordination with the LGR programme board and HR leads from partner councils ensures recruitment decisions align with emerging service models and reduces the risk of creating unnecessary posts.” 120.5 The Cabinet Member for Finance and Major Projects moved, and the Cabinet Member for Culture and Wellbeing seconded the recommendations for the reasons set out in the report. 120.6 RESOLVED to: 1) Note the forecast £84,522 underspend on the General Fund revenue account and the £207,764 overspend on the Housing Revenue Account (HRA). 2) Note the forecast £12,895,652 underspend against the General Fund and the £6,927,195 underspend against the HRA capital programmes 3) Note the current position of the General Fund and HRA earmarked reserves as set out in Appendix 1 4) Approves the addition of £119,000 to the 2025-2026 General Fund capital programmes, funded wholly by external or ringfenced resources as set out in section 4. Cabinet: 11 February 2026 121. Corporate Risk Register 2025-2026 – Quarter Three 121.1 The Cabinet Member for Finance and Major Projects presented the report. The report detailed the Council’s Corporate Risk Register for quarter three of 2025- 2026. Cabinet was asked to note direction of travel. The position at the end of quarter two had been reported to Cabinet in November. The Council had updated its risk management strategy which had been presented to the Audit Committee and approved by Cabinet. This had been implemented for quarter three. The risk register therefore included a refreshed risk scoring and a risk appetite score for each risk. All risks had been reviewed and details were included in paragraph 3 of the report. There had been no significant change to the Council’s risk profile and the environment in which the Council operated remained high risk including in relation to funding. Progress would continue to be reported to Cabinet. 121.2 Councillor Galvin asked the following question: “CORP38 is the Devolution and Local Government Reorganisation. Given the huge impacts, costs and risks, it is good this is included - but what exactly is this risk measuring, and how do financial pressures form part of corporate risks considered when calculating this metric?” 121.3 The Cabinet Member for Finance and Major Projects gave the following response: “The new risk strategy was rolled out to risk owners during Q3 of the 2025/26 financial year. The risk strategy includes a risk template to help risk owners better describe a risk and score it using an “If”, “Then”, “Resulting In” method. CORP38 is measuring NCC’s work to ensure a smooth transition into whatever new authority is established, ensuring, through the transition process, that statutory services continue to be delivered and that our communities receive a good standard of service, whilst balancing this with the work needed to ensure we contribute positively to the creation of the new Authority/ies. This means that the risk focuses on multiple areas around budgets, planning, resourcing, working in partnership across Norfolk, governance and communications and most importantly our staff. Financial pressures will be considered when assessing our risk appetite in accordance with the new risk strategy, as well as in evaluating current risk levels. This risk will be reviewed regularly, and interventions will be made if the risk score is not deemed acceptable. It is widely recognised that homelessness and rough sleeping are complex issues that cannot be addressed by the local authority in isolation. In Norwich, we are fortunate to have a wide range of organisations and charities working alongside us to support some of our most vulnerable residents. Within the action plan that accompanies this strategy, delivery partners are identified alongside the NCC Housing team, setting out clear accountability for each action. The action plan will be reviewed, reported on and updated annually to Cabinet: 11 February 2026 ensure it remains relevant and that accountability is maintained. As part of this process, relevant partners will be engaged to contribute to and support this work, in addition to ongoing ‘business as usual’ partnership and collaboration.” 121.4 The Cabinet Member for Finance and Major Projects moved, and the Cabinet Member for Equalities and Social Justice seconded the recommendations for the reasons set out in the report. 121.5 RESOLVED to note the identified risks and the direction of travel, 122. Homelessness and Rough Sleeping Strategy 2026-2031 122.1 The Cabinet Member for Housing presented the report. The Council had a duty to update its Homelessness Strategy. The updated Homelessness and Rough Sleeping Strategy had brought together a number of existing strategy to create comprehensive joined up approach and acknowledged that homelessness extended beyond rough sleeping. Increased private rented sector costs and a shortage of affordable housing had created new demand on the Council’s services which drove homelessness. The Council was taking a new preventative approach which was aligned with the Government’s approach. The strategy set out an overall vision and priorities with an action plan which guided work over the next five years by working with partners to deliver support to residents. The action plan would be reviewed and updated annually. 122.2 Councillor Galvin asked the following question: “Thank you for this updated strategy. Homelessness continues to be a huge and growing challenge, and thanks are due to all the teams who work to help in this area. Could you explain a bit more about how key delivery partnerships in the city, for example NGOs and providers, will be involved in ongoing monitoring and evaluation of the strategy?” 122.3 The Cabinet Member for Housing gave the following response: “It is widely recognised that homelessness and rough sleeping are complex issues that cannot be addressed by the local authority in isolation. In Norwich, we are fortunate to have a wide range of organisations and charities working alongside us to support some of our most vulnerable residents. Within the action plan that accompanies this strategy, delivery partners are identified alongside the NCC Housing team, setting out clear accountability for each action. The action plan will be reviewed, reported on and updated annually to ensure it remains relevant and that accountability is maintained. As part of this process, relevant partners will be engaged to contribute to and support this work, in addition to ongoing ‘business as usual’ partnership and collaboration.” 122.4 The Cabinet Member commented that there had been involvement in the development of the strategy from people with lived experiences to ensure their voices had been heard. Partners across all areas had experience of working with residents with complex needs. The Council worked with partners through constructive forums both on an formal and informal basis. Cabinet: 11 February 2026 122.5 The Cabinet Member for Housing moved, and the Cabinet Member for Culture and Wellbeing seconded the recommendations for the reasons set out in the report. 122.6 RESOLVED to approve and adopt the Homelessness and Rough Sleeping Strategy 2026-2031. 123. Revisions to the Home Options Policy 123.1 The Cabinet Member for Housing presented the report. The Policy had been considered by the Scrutiny Committee which had made a number of recommendations that were detailed in the report. The Home Options policy had last been updated in 2021 and required an update to legislation and ensured that the policy addressed housing needs. The amendments were limited in scope and included new guidance, legislation and a plan to end homelessness. She welcomed the debate from the Scrutiny Committee which had been helpful as portfolio holder. A recommendation from the Scrutiny Committee had not been accepted as it was a long-standing provision that silver band was not awarded where a situation had arisen due to tenants’ own choice. Other options to seek alternative accommodation such as mutual exchange. 123.2 Councillor Galvin asked the following question: “Scrutiny Committee resolved to ask that Cabinet remove the section that sets out that silver band for no garden access will not be awarded for those children who were born when the current property was accepted. This was for reasons including that children should not be punished for their parents' decisions, and that as children grow up perhaps parents might realise that they need a garden when they did not foresee this. The Portfolio Holder has not accepted this because they say the applicant’s housing circumstances have been ‘created through their own decisions and choices’ - although this is clearly not the children’s decision. What actions will you take to make sure that this policy does not act to the detriment of children, keeping them stuck inside for their childhoods (for example, can we facilitate a better exchange process?)” 123.3 The Cabinet Member for Housing gave the following response: “While I appreciate the concerns raised, it is important to recognise that many hundreds of thousands of families across the country successfully and happily raise children in flats. Living in a flat does not mean a child is “stuck inside”; families continue to have access to shared outdoor spaces, local parks, play areas, and wider community facilities. In the specific circumstances being discussed, we are referring to households who made an active choice to move to a property without a garden. In cases where an applicant’s current housing circumstances arise from their own decisions, it is reasonable that they would not receive additional priority through the Home Options scheme for that same issue. However, this does not mean that families are left without routes to move if their needs change. Importantly, Home Options is only one of the mechanisms available. Mutual exchange remains one of the fastest and most effective ways for social housing Cabinet: 11 February 2026 tenants to find a more suitable home. It is widely used and works extremely well in practice: in 2025 alone, 160 council tenant households were able to move through this process. We will continue to support tenants in making best use of these routes, and to promote mutual exchange as a flexible and responsive option for families whose needs evolve over time.” 123.4 The Cabinet Member for Housing moved, and the Cabinet Member for Culture and Wellbeing seconded the recommendations for the reasons set out in the report. 123.5 RESOLVED to agree the adoption of the updated Home Options policy. 124. Norwich Airport Surface Access Strategy 124.1 The Cabinet Member for Planning and Regulatory Services presented the report. The report detailed Norwich Airport Limited’s Surface Access Strategy which had been required by the adopted masterplan and the outline planning consent. The strategy included all land within the operational boundaries and detailed targets and measures for surface access for all current and future tenant businesses. Proposed measures within the strategy included improvements to onsite and offsite infrastructure. The strategy encouraged alternative methods of transport for staff and passengers. The report detailed responses to recommendations made by the Sustainable Development Panel, several of the recommendations were outside the scope of the strategy. The strategy was sufficient to meet the condition of the outline consent. It was acknowledged that the document could be more ambitious in future. The Cabinet would endorse the strategy subject to two conditions, which were that the airport undertook an Equalities Impact Assessment to be distributed to all partner authorities and that the annual monitoring report is reported annually to the Joint Airport Consultative Committee. 124.2 Councillor Padda left the meeting at this point. 124.3 Councillor Galvin asked the following question: “How does the Norwich Airport Surface Access Strategy actively commit to reducing carbon emissions and private car dependency, rather than merely accommodating forecast growth in airport activity, including for example through the use of binding modal-shift targets for public transport, walking and cycling for both staff and passengers, and enforcement mechanisms that will apply if airport growth results in increased overall surface transport emissions?” 124.4 The Cabinet Member for Planning and Regulatory Services gave the following response: “Endorsing the Surface Access Strategy will enable the Council to commit the airport and its tenant businesses to implement the broad range of measures that are set out within it. The targets for sustainable transport have increased significantly compared with those initially proposed, following officer concerns that targets for passengers and staff were not ambitious enough and there was greater scope for modal shift. Cabinet: 11 February 2026 It now contains precise and ambitious commitments from the Airport, which can upon endorsement by the councils be used as a positive baseline position to move forward from, which is a much-improved position from where we are now. Without the strategy if the existing mode share remains unchanged, an additional 2 tonnes of Carbon Dioxide Equivalent (CO2e) emissions would be generated each day by growth at the Airport through additional staff and passenger trips. If the targets set out within this ASAS are realised, it could potentially save 2.1 tonnes of CO2e emissions meaning that the CO2e emissions would be slightly lower than the 2022 base. This represents a reduction in carbon emissions compared to the estimated CO2e emissions in 2022. This would mean that the implementation would result in a decrease in CO2e emissions as a result of Airport growth. Monitoring will be key with the ASAS being monitored on an annual/regular basis. Targets may need to be revised depending on the growth of the airport, the current transport landscape and performance during the preceding year. This will allow more ambitious targets to be agreed as the airport continues to grow, allowing the ASAS to eliminate the transport-related impact of this growth.” 124.5 The Cabinet Member for Planning and Regulatory Services moved, and the Cabinet Member for Culture and Wellbeing seconded the recommendations for the reasons set out in the report. 124.6 RESOLVED to endorse the Airport Surface Access Strategy, subject to the following conditions: 1) That the Airport produce an Equalities Impact Assessment, which is distributed to partner authorities. 2) That the Airport bring their Annual Monitoring Report to the Joint Norwich Airport Consultative Committee annually for discussion. 125. Greater Norwich Five Year Infrastructure Investment Plan 125.1 The Leader of the Council presented the report. The infrastructure investment plan had been prepared to provide a longer-term strategic context for infrastructure investment decisions while eliminating the need to approve individual projects at Cabinet meetings of all partner authorities more than once a year. The projects in the plan were considered a priority for delivery to assist in achieving economic growth targets in Greater Norwich Local Plan (GNLP) and the Greater Norwich City Deal. The plan had been considered by the Greater Norwich Growth Board and was being recommended for approval to each district council. The plan included the updated position on infrastructure delivery, revised Community Infrastructure Levy income forecasts and provided updates on projects accepted within previous plans and Annual Growth Programme. Cabinet were asked to note that the Annual Growth Programme contained projects at Woodrow Pilling Park and Yare Valley Walk UEA Boardwalk and that the subject to the approval of the Council’s capital programme by Cabinet and subsequently Council and the proposed use of the Cabinet: 11 February 2026 remaining £25.5million reduced-cost City Deal Borrowing which was set to expire at the end of March 2026. 125.2 Councillor Galvin asked the following question: “In October the Council discussed seemingly behind closed doors options for utilising the remaining £25.5m of City Deal Borrowing by the end of March 2026 as the Treasury was unwilling to extend its deadline for drawing down the money. None of the three district councils have got projects on which to spend the money despite the end date being known about since 2014. As a result, the proposal is to agree a Key Decision to allow Norfolk County Council to utilise the remaining £18.5m of borrowing flexibly within their borrowing requirements. To date, the City Deal borrowing spent has gone on environmentally damaging improvements to the road network. Please will the leader detail exactly how he will ensure that the remaining monies will be spent on infrastructure projects which benefit the environment and the large number of city residents living in deprivation?” 125.3 The Leader of the Council gave the following response: “The Greater Norwich Growth Board is a well‑regarded partnership between the four local authorities in the Greater Norwich area. It isn’t something we’re legally required to have — the councils chose to work together so we can plan and deliver the infrastructure needed for growth in a coordinated, transparent way. When we talk about “planned growth”, we’re referring to the Greater Norwich Local Plan, which was formally adopted in March 2024. All decisions about the Infrastructure Investment Fund and the Five‑Year Infrastructure Investment Plan are based directly on what that Local Plan requires. The borrowing we’re talking about here comes from the original City Deal agreement with Government. That deal offered reduced‑cost borrowing, but only on the basis that the Greater Norwich authorities worked together to deliver the Joint Core Strategy — the previous version of today’s Local Plan — and the supporting infrastructure. Because of that, the borrowing is ring‑fenced. It can only be used for specific types of infrastructure: education, green infrastructure, community facilities and transport. It cannot be used for anything else. There are several types of borrowing within the City Deal. The £18.5 million discussed here relates to borrowing that hasn’t yet been taken up, often because major infrastructure projects have changed or been delayed over time. It’s important to stress that this is borrowing, not funding — it must be repaid. All of the district councils were asked if they wished to take it on, and all declined. Norfolk County Council has therefore stepped in as the borrower. Crucially, although the County Council could legally use this borrowing more widely, it has chosen to limit it to the same categories of infrastructure the Growth Board itself would have applied. So the principles and priorities remain the same. A good example of how City Deal borrowing has been used in the past is the Broadland Northway. Although it’s a road scheme, it was essential to unlocking the Cabinet: 11 February 2026 largest growth area in our region — enabling new homes, including affordable housing, new community facilities, employment land and supporting services. It also paved the way for Broadland Country Park, a significant new green space funded through the Growth Board, which simply wouldn’t have happened otherwise. This shows the “whole‑place” approach the Growth Board takes: making sure that homes, jobs, transport, green spaces and community facilities all come forward together in a balanced and environmentally responsible way.” 125.4 The Leader of the Council moved, and the Deputy Leader and Cabinet Member for Climate and Environment seconded the recommendations for the reasons set out in the report. 125.5 RESOLVED to approve the draft Five-Year Infrastructure Investment Plan 2026-2031 (see Appendix A) which included: • The proposed 2026/27 Annual Growth Programme (AGP), noting that the AGP contains projects at Woodrow Pilling Park and Yare Valley Walk UEA Boardwalk and that the allocation of funding for these projects is subject to the approval of the Council’s capital programme by Cabinet and subsequently Council in the associated budget papers. • The proposed use of the remaining £25.5m reduced-cost City Deal Borrowing, which is set to expire at the end of March 2026. 112. Draft Affordable Housing Supplementary Planning Document (SPD) 112.1 The Cabinet Member for Planning and Regulatory Services presented the report. The draft Supplementary Planning Document (SPD) supported the application of Policy 5 of the Greater Norwich Local Plan (GNLP) which required 33% affordable housing and 28% affordable housing for the city centre. The delivery of affordable housing should be onsite unless exceptional circumstances justified off-site provision. The SPD detailed how the off-site provision would be calculated. The draft SPD retained control over how s106 funds were spent. The Council received £1.9million in s106 commuted funds which had enabled the delivery of 700 affordable homes, including Goldsmith Street, the Mile Cross depot site and Argyle Street. 112.2 Councillor Galvin asked the following question: “Given the deepening affordability and climate emergency, it is disappointing that the draft Affordable Housing SPD continues to prioritise viability flexibility for developers over firm, non-negotiable delivery of genuinely affordable, low-carbon homes. Will Cabinet commit to strengthening the SPD so that social rent, zero-carbon standards, and long-term affordability are treated as core planning requirements rather than optional outcomes subject to negotiation?” 112.3 The Cabinet Member for Planning and Regulatory Services gave the following response: Cabinet: 11 February 2026 “The SPD cannot set new policy and must accord with the Greater Norwich Local Plan and national policy. All development proposals should be fully policy compliant unless it can be demonstrated through a full viability assessment that this is not possible. Whilst the role for viability assessment is primarily at the plan making stage, both the national Planning Policy Guidance and policy 5 of the GNLP include the provision for viability testing at the planning application stage to reflect case by case differences and differences over time. It is up to the applicant to demonstrate whether particular circumstances justify the need for a viability assessment. Policy 2 of the GNLP seeks to ensure that development proposals have low levels of energy consumption. This is therefore not an issue that can be addressed through the Affordable Housing SPD as the Affordable Housing SPD only supplements policy 5 of the GNLP. The Future Homes Standard which is due to come into effect later in the year is aimed at enhancing the energy performance of new homes.” 112.4 The Cabinet Member for Planning and Regulatory Services moved, and the Deputy Leader and Cabinet Member for Climate and Environment seconded the recommendations for the reasons set out in the report. 112.5 RESOLVED to: 1) Recommend that Full Council agree to go out for consultation on the draft Supplementary Planning Document (SPD) 2) Delegate sign off of any minor amendments to the draft SPD prior to public consultation to the Head of Planning in consultation with the Portfolio Holder for Planning and Regulatory Services as appropriate. 113. Award of two HRA maintenance contracts 113.1 The Cabinet Member for Housing presented the report. The contracts for consideration were to support the management of the Council’s hosing stock, which were annual gas safety checks and electrical tests. Contracts were currently in place but were due to expire in March and therefore contracts were required from April 2026. The Council had reviewed the contracts to ensure that it continued to meet the Council’s and residents’ needs. The work would be linked to other activity such as damp and mould to work closely with contractors. The contractors had been identified through frameworks. 113.2 There were no questions from group leaders submitted in advance of the meeting. 113.3 The Cabinet Member for Housing moved, and the Deputy Leader and Cabinet Member for Climate and Environment seconded the recommendations for the reasons set out in the report. 113.4 RESOLVED: Cabinet: 11 February 2026 113.5 To approve the awards of the contract for Domestic & District Gas Servicing as contained in Exempt Appendix A, (Recommendation 1) and Domestic Electrical Inspections and Testing (Recommendation 2), under the Housing Revenue Account (HRA) maintenance programme at a total value of £12,750,000.00 following completion of the process as prescribed within the relevant frameworks: Item Action Works Programme Value 1 Award New contract for Domestic & District Gas Servicing and Repairs to a single supplier, CONTRACTOR A, for the period 01 April 2026 for up to five years to 31 March 2031. £11,000,000.00 2 Award Domestic Electrical Inspections and Testing (EICRs) to a single supplier, CONTRACTOR A, for the period 01 April 2026 for up to five years to 31 March 2031. £1,750,000.00 114. Exclusion of the Public 114.1 RESOLVED to exclude the press and public from the meeting during the consideration of the below items of the exempt report on the grounds that they contained exempt information as defined in the relevant paragraphs within Part 1 of Schedule 12A, as amended, of the Local Government Act 1972. 115. Disposal of Assets (Housing) (Para 3) 115.1 (An exempt minutes exists for this item). 115.2 The Cabinet Member for Housing moved, and the Deputy Leader and Cabinet Member for Climate and Environment seconded the recommendations for the reasons set out in the report. 115.3 RESOLVED that the following recommendations were accepted as detailed in the report. 115.4 (An exempt minute exists for this item). CHAIR Cabinet: 11 February 2026 Appendix A Cabinet 11 February 2026 Questions to cabinet members Question 1 Councillor Stutely to ask the cabinet member for planning and regulatory services the following question: “The planning condition requiring a Surface Access Strategy set a minimum requirement but allowed scope for the Council to require a more ambitious and comprehensive approach to mitigation and sustainability, as is common practice at many other regional airports. While officers will have advised on what would satisfy that condition, could the Cabinet Member confirm that Cabinet is content to limit the scope of the Strategy to soft surface-access measures, rather than requiring a more ambitious package of mitigation and local benefit?” Councillor Giles, the cabinet member for planning and regulatory services' response: “Planning condition 26 of application 21/0011901/O requires the airport to produce a surface access strategy covering how people access the airport along with the Masterplan endorsed by the Council in 2019. The requirements can only relate to the access strategy in a defined area and not the operation of the Airport as a whole. Looking at the progress made, it is felt that the ASAS contains precise and ambitious commitments, which can be used as a positive baseline position to move forward from, which is a much-improved position from where we are now. Measures include a combination of onsite and off-site infrastructure and promotional measures. The ASAS includes measures for Norwich Airport Ltd staff and passengers and for the tenant businesses. The ASAS is ambitious with specific but achievable targets and measures. It is important that all measures are within scope. Requiring the airport to incorporate measures outside scope would be unreasonable. This is a live document and after endorsement progress towards delivering mode share targets will be monitored through an officer group from Norwich, Broadland and Norfolk County Council. This is in addition to formally reviewing the strategy annually with targets being amended as appropriate with the agreement of all parties.” Supplementary Question Cabinet: 11 February 2026 By way of a supplementary question Councillor Stutely asked whether the Cabinet Member believed that the level of ambition within the Surface Access Strategy was proportionate to the growth, health and wellbeing and environmental interests when other regional airports had considered mode targets and other mitigation targets. In response the Cabinet Member for Planning and Regulatory Services said that the Strategy addressed the surface access to the airport. Other impacts of emissions and how to address these would be done through partnership work. There was provision within the Strategy for the target to become more ambitious over time. Other regional airports had been able to introduce things such as an offsetting fund as there were larger and had more funds. It was better to reduce carbon emissions at the source rather than to offset these. The Strategy addressed monitoring while recognising that this was complex when only considering surface access. Therefore a diverse mix of tools were being used to monitor progress including the completion of projects.

documents.title: Home Options Allocation Scheme 2026 (adopted policy)
documents.text: Home Options Allocation Scheme 2026 On this page Summary of changes 1. Introduction 2. Application Procedure 3. The housing need bands 4. Methods of assessment 5. Accessing the housing options 6. Statement on equal access 7. Reviews of decisions 8. Confidentiality statement 9. Monitoring/changes to the scheme Appendix A Appendix B Appendix C Appendix D Appendix E If you need this information by email for use with the read-aloud function or in an alternative format, please contact us on 0344 980 3333 or visit norwich.gov.uk/intran Published 12 February 2026 Summary of changes Norwich City Council has updated its Home Options housing allocations policy to ensure it remains compliant with current legislation and reflects the needs of local residents. The policy, which determines how social housing is prioritised and allocated in Norwich was last reviewed in October 2021. The proposed revisions are relatively minor but incorporate recent changes in law, statutory guidance, and national strategies including the Government’s National Plan to End Homelessness. These updates have been shaped through a public consultation which took place in Autumn 2025 and scrutiny by the council’s Overview and Scrutiny Committee.’ In accordance with statutory guidance and to ensure that the council’s housing policies benefit local people, applicants must have been continuously resident in Norwich for at least the last two years. Exceptions, as set down in legislation, will apply. The number of refusals allowed before an application is reviewed and potentially cancelled for 12 months will be reduced from five to three to reflect extremely high demand for social housing. This will not apply to homelessness clients, who, as required by legislation, receive one offer. Clarification of priority banding for rough sleepers: where it has been confirmed that an applicant is sleeping rough, meets the qualification criteria and it has been assessed that there is no other accommodation available to them, silver band will be awarded by the council’s rough sleeper team. The team will carry out a needs-led assessment and use professional judgement to engage and support people sleeping rough in each case. Priority will not be awarded when the client does not engage with the council’s support or where accommodation has been made available to the applicant which they have chosen not to accept. In accordance with the Armed Forces Covenant, U.K. armed forces veterans will be prioritised within bands. You can view the details of the public consultation on Get Talking Norwich , which closed on 7 December 2025. The consultation was combined with the Homelessness Strategy. 1. Introduction 1.1.1. This allocation policy explains the rules that determine how Norwich City Council (known throughout this document as ‘the council’) allocates social housing properties. It sets out the priorities and procedures that the council will follow in the letting of social housing to applicants on its housing register. 1.1.2. The Registered Providers (Housing Associations) that are part of the scheme are known throughout this document as ‘scheme landlords’. These are listed in Appendix A . 1.2. Background 1.2.1. The allocation scheme is also known as Home Options. Under the scheme, the council and scheme landlords advertise their properties for rent on a weekly basis on its website and invite bids on each property from applicants who are registered with the scheme. 1.2.2. Norwich is an area of very high housing need and demand for social housing far exceeds the supply of accommodation that becomes available. It must be remembered that Home Options does not produce any more affordable housing but provides a fairer, more efficient and transparent way of allocating the social housing available. 1.3. Scheme objectives 1.3.1. The key objectives of the scheme are to: Meet the legal requirements for the allocation of social housing. Focus resources on those in the most need. Operate a scheme which is, fair, transparent and easy to use. Help meet the housing needs of Norwich residents . Allow scheme users, through the transparent nature of the scheme, to make informed decisions about their housing options. Make best use of Norwich’s social housing stock. Encourage and support, balanced and sustainable communities. Prevent homelessness and reduce the use of temporary accommodation. Encourage through flow from hostel accommodation in order to reduce rough sleeping. Operate the scheme so that it improves accessibility and customer service for vulnerable groups in Norwich. Make sure those who have the greatest need for housing have the greatest opportunity to get it. Pay due regard to the aims of the Norwich Homelessness Strategy and Tenancy Strategy. Meet the council’s corporate priorities of ensuring a fairer city. 1.4. Legal framework 1.4.1. This allocation scheme complies with the legal framework for allocating social housing, laid down in the Housing Act 1996 and takes account of statutory government guidance on the allocation of accommodation. 1.4.2. This allocation scheme pays due regard to the Equality Act 2010. 1.4.3. The assessment of eligibility, qualification and assessment of priority for the Home Options scheme will take into account any changes to legislation made subsequent to this policy. 1.5. How does the scheme work? 1.5.1. Home Options is a choice-based lettings scheme. The council and scheme landlords advertise their vacant properties to those on the housing register. The adverts include a detailed description of the property. Applicants on the register can then bid for the property of their choice if they are eligible and meet the qualifying criteria. 1.5.2. The successful applicant will be selected from those who have bid for the property and meet the stated qualifying criteria. Selection will be based on the highest band, followed by the banding date where there is more than one applicant from the same band. 1.5.3. Feedback will be provided on what demand there was for previously advertised properties. This will help applicants to make informed choices. 1.5.4. This policy is available free of charge at the website www.norwich.gov.uk. A paper copy of the full policy is available upon request from City Hall at a cost of £25.00. 2. Application Procedure 2.1. How to apply 2.1.1. To apply for a social housing property in Norwich an applicant must be registered with Home Options. 2.1.2. Applications to Home Options can be made over the telephone on 0344 980 3333. All applications will involve a discussion of an applicant’s housing need with an adviser. Acceptance onto Home Options register is not a guarantee that an applicant will be offered accommodation. Home-Options is unable to meet the needs of all home-seekers and transferring tenants looking for accommodation. Applicants who do not meet the criteria for a priority banding category are extremely unlikely to be rehoused through the Home Options scheme and will be given advice about alternative housing options. 2.1.3. Home Options is a scheme which is based on verification. All applicants will be required to provide evidence of their household circumstances including income, savings and housing history. 2.1.4. Information to support an application may be asked for at any time. If the information is not provided, the application may be suspended or removed from Home-Options and any offers of accommodation withdrawn. All applicants will be offered help and advice to complete their application. This includes translation and interpreting facilities where required. 2.2. Who can apply? 2.2.1. Residents of the UK who are over 18 years old can apply to Home Options however this does not guarantee an application will be taken or that the applicant will be re-housed under the scheme. 2.2.2. By law, there are defined groups of applicants who cannot be re-housed through the scheme. There are also exceptions or restrictions to an application which may apply. 2.2.3. Under the Housing Act 1996, local authorities must consider whether applicants are eligible for housing assistance. The council will apply the relevant legislation that is in place at the time of application. 2.3. The applicant’s household 2.3.1. The council will decide in each case as to whether the people included in the application by the applicant will be considered as a part of the household for purposes of assessing housing need. 2.3.2. Any person wishing to be included as part of an applicant’s household must satisfy the Council that they are a permanent member of the applicant’s household and show that it is reasonable to expect them to reside with the applicant on a continuing basis. 2.3.3. The council will not consider the following as members of an applicant’s household: Anyone who falls within legislation prohibiting them from having recourse to public funds or is an asylum seeker Non-dependent children who have not lived within the household continually throughout their adult lives Relatives who do not form part of the applicant’s immediate family where there is no formal care arrangement; parents or step-parents, grandparents, brothers or step-brothers, sisters or step-sisters, aunts, uncles, grandchildren, nieces, nephews, cousins. Any family member not resident in the UK at the time of the application. Any person who does not meet eligibility criteria Friends and acquaintances Lodgers Live in help Students living away from home with their own rent liability 2.3.4. Only dependent children that form a permanent part of the household can be considered. Only if an applicant is evidenced to have their child stay with them for four or more nights a week can they be classed as part of the applicant’s household when making an assessment. Temporary arrangements or contact arrangements cannot be considered and household size will be determined upon evidence that any living arrangements are permanent, and the applicant can demonstrate to the council’s satisfaction that they have full-time, permanent responsibility for the child. Where a formal residence agreement is not in place, the council will consider: Confirmation from the Courts regarding residency or parental responsibility. Who the children usually live with Who has financial responsibility for the children The length of time any arrangement has been in place Where the children go to school Any other relevant information 2.3.5. In cases where an applicant wishes to include their children in their Home Options application, this will not be considered where those children have adequate accommodation available to them elsewhere, for example with another parent. 2.3.6. Household members can only appear on one Home Options application. 2.3.7. Households that have been accepted to adopt or foster a child will be assessed as if they have assumed parental responsibility upon written confirmation from Norfolk County Council being provided. 2.3.8. Where an applicant feels that an additional bedroom is needed for a carer, this can only be considered where we have evidence of the need for permanent 24 hour care from a non-family member who is not part of the household and requires their own bedroom to sleep in on a continuing basis. ‘Waking care’ will not be taken into consideration. We would expect that the applicant would be in receipt of Carer’s Allowance and Disability Living Allowance/Personal Independent Payment with the highest care/enhanced rate component. The carer must be recognised, employed by, or working on behalf of Adult Social Care and we would expect them to be a named person (unless your care is provided on a rota arrangement made by Adult Social Care or an agency on their behalf). The decision will be made by the assessment panel. 2.3.9. Where the family unit is not currently residing together, the assessment will be based on the part of the household that occupies accommodation that provides them with the most suitable housing providing there is a reasonable expectation that they should reside together. 2.3.10. Where an applicant has been assessed in accordance with the Mental Capacity Act 2005 as being unable to hold or to manage a tenancy, they may be suspended from the register until a suitable advocate is appointed to act on their behalf. 2.3.11. For an applicant to become a tenant and enter into a tenancy agreement, they must have the mental capacity to understand the contract. If an applicant does not have the capacity to understand the contract, an application should be made to the Court of Protection by an advocate for the tenancy agreement to be signed on their behalf. 2.3.12. Unborn children will not be considered as part of the assessment. A child cannot be added to an application until the applicant has provided a copy of the birth certificate. 2.3.13. For people in prison, applications can be made within 8 weeks of release if the client meets qualification and local connection criteria. In such instances the client does not need to apply for housing in person and applications will be accepted from a third party on behalf of a person in custody, for example by a Prison Resettlement Officer as part of a Resettlement Plan where third-party consent has been given. 2.3.14. Only household members that meet the eligibility and qualification criteria set out in this policy will be included in an application. 2.4. Eligibility 2.4.1. The Home Options team will determine the eligibility of an applicant, based on immigration status and habitual residence, by applying the legislation that is in place at the time of the application and the point of allocation. 2.4.2. Eligibility for Home Options depends on where the applicant normally lives (‘habitual residence’) and their immigration status. A person is not eligible if they are: subject to immigration control (with limited exceptions) classed as an ineligible person from abroad a person not habitually resident in the United Kingdom or required to leave the UK by the Secretary of State. 2.4.3. Eligibility is explained in detail within statutory guidance – online at: Allocation of accommodation: guidance for local authorities - GOV.UK 2.4.4. Eligibility for housing assistance can be affected if there is a change in the immigration status of the applicant(s), and therefore eligibility for an allocation of housing will be kept under review. The applicant is responsible for informing the council of any change in their immigration status. 2.4.5. Applicants whose households include a person from abroad who is ineligible will not be afforded priority if they are only homeless or in housing need as a consequence of the presence of the ineligible person. 2.5. Qualification for housing in Norwich 2.5.1. The Localism Act 2011 allows councils to make local decisions about who qualifies for social housing in their area in order to ensure that local objectives and the needs of local residents are met. 2.5.2. The decision that an applicant does not qualify for an allocation may occur at the time of joining the Home Options scheme, at any time during the life of the application, at the time the applicant is allocated a property, or when the applicant has bid and has been short-listed for a property. The Home Options team will make the decision. 2.5.3. In accordance with statutory guidance and to ensure that the council’s housing policies benefit local people, applicants must have been continuously resident in Norwich for at least the last two years. If applicants cannot provide satisfactory evidence that they meet the criteria, an application will not be taken. For household members to join an application and to be included in any assessment of housing need, the same criteria apply. 2.5.4. Exceptional circumstances will be considered. In such cases, the decision as to whether an applicant qualifies will be determined by a Housing Options team leader or manager, or by the council’s assessment panel. 2.5.5. Examples are: Somebody who needs to live in Norwich as they have a significant need to be near specific medical care which is unavailable elsewhere. Applicants over 60 who have a specific need for sheltered housing in Norwich to be near medical care or family support unavailable elsewhere. The applicant needs to move to Norwich where failure to meet that need would cause extreme hardship to themselves or others. Tenants of social housing needing to move to Norwich for work-related reasons where failure to meet that need would cause hardship, who can evidence that they meet the criteria set out in the 2015 Regulations (SI 2015/967). Care leavers – Applicants aged 18-21 years (or up to 25 years old if they are pursuing a programme of education agreed in their pathway plan), who are owed a duty under Children Act 1989, section 23C. Applicants fleeing domestic abuse who are living in refuge accommodation or who need to move urgently for the safety and security of themselves and any dependent children. Applicants that can demonstrate a lifelong residential connection to Norwich which has been broken for only a short time. These are examples and this list is not exhaustive. 2.5.6. Residents in prison, bail hostel, hospital or approved premises, or those households referred into or placed into any form of accommodation in Norwich by another agency or local authority will not gain a local connection and time spent in such premises will not count toward local connection. 2.5.7. Applicants whose only residential connection to Norwich is through further education or student accommodation will not be considered as having gained local connection. Student accommodation is that provided by an educational establishment or where a student exemption certificate has been provided for council tax purposes. 2.5.8. Where an applicant has only become eligible for housing assistance in the last two years, their local connection will commence from the date they became eligible. 2.5.9. Where an application is taken from a client who has not lived in Norwich continuously for the previous two years, and the client would normally be placed in a priority band, a ‘reduced preference’ will apply until the two year connection is established. 2.6. Exception to the criteria: Armed and Reserve Forces 2.6.1. The council is committed to ensuring that service personnel and their families have access to appropriate accommodation when they leave the British armed forces. Under the terms of the Armed Forces Covenant, to which the council is signatory, the local connection criteria will not apply to the following: Those who are currently serving in the regular forces or who have served in the regular forces. Bereaved spouses or civil partners of those serving in the armed and reserve forces where (i) the bereaved spouse or civil partner has recently ceased or will cease to be entitled to reside in Ministry of Defence accommodation following the death of their spouse or civil partner and (ii) the death was wholly or partly attributable to their service. Existing or former members of the reserve forces who are suffering from a serious injury, illness or disability which is wholly or partly attributable to their service. Divorced or separated spouses or civil partners of Service personnel who are required to move out of accommodation provided by the Ministry of Defence. Under these terms, the council can ensure that current and former service personnel in urgent housing need are awarded preference in line with the priority need bands. 2.7. Those who will not qualify: need considerations 2.7.1. Home Options policy aims to manage expectations realistically and to focus resources on those in most need of them. Therefore, having considered the provisions made in the Localism Act 2011, the following applicants will not qualify: Applicants who are tenants of scheme landlords who have made a ‘right to buy’ application on their property. Applicants who are tenants of scheme landlords and are in the process of carrying out a mutual exchange or have completed a mutual exchange in the previous 12 months. Applicants who have been housed through the scheme will not be able to reapply for Home Options for a 12-month period from the commencement of their new tenancy. This restriction does not apply where the household circumstances have changed and the property is no longer suitable or where there are extenuating circumstances. Applicants who have been housed through the council’s private sector leasing scheme (Let NCC) or through a loan from the council’s Homelessness Prevention Fund will have their Home Options application cancelled and will not be able to reapply for a 12-month period from the commencement of their new tenancy. This restriction does not apply where the household circumstances have changed and the property is no longer suitable or where there are extenuating circumstances. Clients who have been sponsored to enter the country in the last five years based on an undertaking given by a sponsor that accommodation was available (and where that sponsor is still alive). Applicants who own or have an interest in a property as a freeholder, leaseholder, a part-owner through shared ownership, including part commercial/residential property, in the UK or abroad will not qualify unless there are extenuating circumstances, as determined by a review panel. Examples of extenuating circumstances could be someone who requires sheltered housing in Norwich. 2.8. Those who will not qualify: behaviour considerations 2.8.1. The council, scheme landlords and Norwich residents have a right to expect certain standards of behaviour. Where an applicant or a member of their household has a history of behaviour which is evidenced to have caused a detrimental effect to others, the Council may decide that the applicant does not qualify to be accepted onto the Home Options scheme. 2.8.2. Some examples of the type of behaviour that could mean that an applicant does not qualify for the Home Options scheme are: Serious rent arrears which, in the council’s view, would entitle the landlord to a possession order. Causing deliberate damage to a property. Causing anti-social behaviour such as nuisance to neighbours, discriminatory behaviour or harassment, abuse, violence, or intimidation to the community or to council staff. Conviction for using or allowing a property to be used for illegal or immoral purposes. Committing domestic abuse. Conviction for violent crime or the supply, use or possession of drugs. Conviction of a criminal offence in the property or in the locality of the property . Eviction from hostel or temporary accommodation . Being convicted of, issued with, or accepted a sanction for Benefit or Council Tax fraud within the last five years. Making a false statement in order to obtain accommodation. Failing to provide relevant information that has been reasonably requested to verify an application for housing Failing to allow contractors to enter the property to carry out maintenance. Requesting or colluding with a landlord or family member to issue them with a Notice to Quit. These are examples and this list is not exhaustive. 2.8.3. The examples relate to both current and former tenancies and apply no matter who the landlord is, when they happened or what form of tenancy was held. Paragraphs 15.3 & 15.4, together with Appendix B , deal with the way in which applicants may demonstrate that they have addressed past behaviour in order to requalify. 2.8.4. Decisions are made on a case-by-case basis, with each case judged on its own merits. 2.9. Public protection arrangements 2.9.1. Applicants subject to multi-agency public protection arrangements can only access the register with the consent of the Housing Options manager. Each case will be considered on its own merits in determining whether an application will be accepted. 2.10. Assessment of applications 2.11. Legal background 2.11.1. All applicants who are eligible and who qualify for Home Options will be placed in the appropriate banding based on an assessment of their housing needs. This is to ensure that the council allocates homes to those in the greatest assessed need and to ensure that its legal obligations are met. 2.11.2. The council is required by law to give reasonable preference in the scheme to people with high levels of assessed housing need: People who need to move on welfare or medical grounds (including grounds relating to a disability). People who need to move to a particular locality of the city to avoid hardship to themselves or others. People living in unsanitary, unsatisfactory, or overcrowded housing, and People who are homeless within the meaning of the Housing Act 1996, and people who are owed a particular statutory duty by any local housing authority under section 190(2), 193(2) or 195(2) (or under section 65(2) or 68(2) of the Housing Act 1985 or who are occupying accommodation secured by any such authority under section 192(3). Former and serving members of the armed or reserve forces who have an urgent housing need or need to move because of a serious injury, medical condition or disability sustained as a result of their service. Bereaved spouses and civil partners of members of the armed forces leaving services family accommodation following the death of their spouse or partner. 2.11.3. Applicants outside the reasonable preference categories can also be given additional consideration to meet local priorities. 2.11.4. Applications are processed by the council’s Home Options team, in accordance with this policy. 3. The housing need bands 3.1. Each application will be assessed to determine the level of housing need of the household and placed into one of five bands: Emergency band - Emergency priority Gold band - High Priority Silver band - Medium priority Bronze band - Emergency/high/medium priority but with reduced preference Standard band - No priority 3.2. Banding will only be awarded where the applicant’s circumstances have been verified. 3.3. An applicant’s circumstances and therefore their level of housing need and banding is subject to change. As such, an applicant’s Home Options banding is kept under continuous review. 3.4. Every applicant is responsible for ensuring that they provide correct and up to date information. 3.5. The criteria for being placed in each band are as follows: 3.6. Emergency band 3.6.1. This band is intended to meet the needs of applicants in extreme circumstances and will only be issued in certain situations where an applicant needs urgent re-housing to ensure their well-being or safety. An applicant in Emergency band is expected to place two bids per week with the guidance of their housing adviser and accept the first suitable available property which they successfully bid for. As examples, circumstances where emergency status may be awarded include: An applicant has an extremely urgent medical need, as determined by a Housing Options team leader or manager or the council’s assessment panel. Those applicants requiring urgent hospital discharge where their current accommodation is totally unsuitable for their needs. Those applicants required to leave their homes as a result of an emergency prohibition order served in relation to the premises under the Housing Act 2004 or as the result of action taken by the Norfolk Fire and Rescue Service. Other extreme circumstances as determined by the Housing Options manager or assessment panel. 3.7. Gold band 3.7.1. Homelessness and homeless prevention: Applicants to whom the council has accepted a prevention of homelessness duty, where their circumstances have been confirmed and who are assessed by their housing adviser as likely to be in priority need. Applicants will have completed and kept to a personalised housing plan made with a housing adviser, will place, or have placed for them, two bids per week with the guidance of their adviser and will be entitled to one suitable offer of accommodation. In such circumstances the need to prevent or relieve homelessness may supersede other housing considerations. Refusal of the offer or failure to engage with advice will mean the council’s duty is ended and gold banding will be removed. 3.7.2. Severe medical need: Critical medical needs directly relating to the applicant’s accommodation or need for accommodation as determined by a Housing Options team leader or manager, or by the council’s assessment panel. Medical priority is only awarded where, in the assessment of the panel, an applicant needs urgent re-housing due to a strongly evidenced, serious and enduring medical condition or disability, which is severely and permanently affected by their current accommodation. Examples of severe medical need determining the award of gold band: The applicant is housebound through mobility issues and moving to alternative accommodation would alleviate this. The applicant’s life is at risk. The applicant is unable to move around their current accommodation, and cannot access kitchen or bathing facilities A member the household is severely disabled and needs substantial adaptations to help meet their needs but these cannot be carried out in their current accommodation. The applicant has a terminal illness and alternative accommodation would allow for suitable care to be provided. The applicant has a severe and enduring medical condition which is significantly exacerbated by poor housing conditions and the accommodation cannot be repaired and no other remedies are available. Armed Forces members and veterans suffering from mental or physical ill health as a result of their service. These are examples and this list is not exhaustive. 3.7.3. Welfare Where the applicant or member of their household assessed by the panel as being grievously and adversely affected by their current accommodation and there is an urgent need to move for welfare reasons. This may include situations such as: Infirmity due to old age The need to give or receive urgent care that cannot be provided by other means A vulnerable applicant is being exploited within their accommodation putting them at risk To help avoid a residential placement where an applicant, with the necessary support mechanisms in place, is capable and best suited to independent living. The applicant is participant is a witness protection programme This list is not exhaustive and other exceptional circumstances will be considered. Assessment will be subject to a thorough investigation of all the circumstances by the council’s assessment panel and the degree of priority awarded will depend on the circumstances of the case. 3.7.4. Housing conditions Applicants have no access to a kitchen and/or bathroom. or A prohibition order or demolition order has been served in relation to the applicant’s dwelling by the council’s private sector housing team. This indicates that the property contains one or more category 1 hazards that probably cannot be remedied. or An improvement notice has been served in relation to the applicant’s dwelling by the private sector housing team and: The remedies that are needed to reduce the hazard will require the property to be vacated for a significant period The cost of the remedies is beyond the means of the applicant (where applicable) The remedies will make the property unsuitable for occupation by the applicant In such cases the award of priority banding is dependent upon individual circumstances, which will be considered on a case-by-case basis by a Housing Options team leader or manager. 3.7.5. Overcrowding Applicants lack two or more bedrooms. 3.7.6. Under-occupation/council interest Tenants of council or scheme landlord accommodation that are under occupying by two or more bedrooms and prepared to move to significantly smaller accommodation or are occupying a substantially adapted property that they no longer require that the housing options manager assesses would be in high demand from applicants in need of those adaptations. 3.7.7. Decommissioning Where a Cabinet decision has been made to decommission a council property, gold band will be awarded to any tenant having to move home as a result. 3.7.8. Violence/Harassment Where there is significant evidence of serious and targeted ongoing harassment or violence toward a household, where a change of accommodation within Norwich could be reasonably expected to alleviate the problem and there is no other remedy. In such instances banding will be awarded by a housing advisor working with the client to prevent their homelessness or as the result of a submission to the assessment panel. 3.7.9. Care leavers Where an applicant is leaving local authority care and is assessed as needing to move on (as determined by a Housing Options team leader or manager following the required evidence and risk assessment being submitted from Children’s Services), where the applicant has completed a tenancy awareness course, support plan outcomes have been met and there is a suitable support package in place so that the council is satisfied that the applicant is able to successfully manage their own tenancy. Referrals can be accepted from four weeks before the applicant leaves care. Applicants will have completed and kept to a personalised housing plan made with a housing adviser, will place two bids per week with the guidance of their adviser and will be entitled to one suitable offer of accommodation. Refusal of the offer will mean that gold banding will be removed. 3.7.10. Let NCC Where the applicant meets the criteria set out under the LetNCC tenant incentive scheme ( Appendix C ) 3.7.11. Multiple Needs Applicants with a combination of medium needs. 3.8. Silver band 3.8.1. Homelessness and homeless prevention Applicants to whom the council has accepted a prevention of homelessness or relief of homelessness duty, where their circumstances have been confirmed and who are assessed by the council’s housing advice team as not likely to be in priority need. Applicants will have completed and kept to a personalised housing plan made with a housing adviser, will place or have placed for them two bids per week with the guidance of their adviser and will be entitled to one offer of accommodation. In such circumstances the need to prevent or relieve homelessness may supersede other housing considerations. Refusal of the offer or failure to engage with advice will mean the council’s duty is ended and silver banding will be removed. 3.8.2. Medical Significant medical needs directly relating to the applicant’s accommodation or need for accommodation as determined by a Housing Options team leader, manager or by the council’s assessment panel. For example: Applicants with an evidenced, enduring, and significant medical or disability problem which seriously affects their ability to manage in their current accommodation, where a move would resolve the issue and no other remedy is available. 3.8.3. Welfare Where, in the assessment of the panel, the applicant or member of their household is evidenced as being seriously and adversely affected by their current accommodation, the issue cannot be remedied and there is a significant need to move for welfare reasons. Assessment will be subject to a thorough investigation of all the circumstances and the degree of priority awarded by the council’s assessment panel will depend on the circumstances of the case. 3.8.4. Housing conditions A hazard awareness notice has been served by the council’s private sector housing team. In relation to a category 1 or 2 hazard at the applicant’s dwelling and: The remedies that are needed to reduce the hazard will require the property to be vacated for a significant period; or The cost of the remedies is beyond the means of the applicant (where applicable); or The remedies will make the property unsuitable for occupation by the applicant A suspended improvement notice or prohibition order exists but a foreseeable change in the applicant’s circumstances will cause it to become active and result in a high priority situation. In such cases the award of priority banding is dependent upon individual circumstances, which will be considered on a case-by-case basis. 3.8.5. Overcrowding Applicants lack one bedroom and those verified as ‘sofa surfing’. 3.8.6. Under-occupation Applicants in general stock council or scheme landlord accommodation, who are under occupying by one bedroom and are willing to move to smaller accommodation. 3.8.7. Children in flats or maisonettes 3.8.7.1 Applicants with a child or children aged ten or under and living in a flat or maisonette that does not have its own garden or private outdoor space. 3.8.7.2 Where a household includes a child or children aged six or under and the applicant lives in a property on the third floor or above where there is no lift access, an extra unit of priority will be added. Please note that any combination of issues related to children in flats would not normally exceed gold band. 3.8.7.3 This category will not be awarded to those households whose children were born when the current accommodation was accepted. 3.8.8. Let NCC Where the applicant meets the criteria set out under the LetNCC tenant incentive scheme ( Appendix C ) 3.8.9. Rough sleeping This priority will be applied where it has been confirmed that an applicant is sleeping rough, meets the qualification criteria (see 2.5) and it has been assessed that there is no other accommodation available to them. The council will carry out a needs-led assessment and use professional judgement to engage and support people sleeping rough in each case. Priority will not be awarded when the client does not engage with the council’s support or where accommodation has been made available to the applicant which they have chosen not to accept. Any banding determination will be made in conjunction with the council’s rough sleeping team. Applicants assessed as ‘sleeping rough’ will not be awarded additional priority on any other accommodation related factors. 3.9. Bronze band (reduced preference) 3.9.1. Reduced preference Applicants with one of the assessed needs as detailed in emergency, gold, or silver band but who have been assessed for reduced preference as set out in section 4.1. In such cases, any criteria applied to the original banding will apply equally once reduced preference has been applied. 3.10. Standard band All other applicants to the scheme will be placed in the standard band: 3.10.1. Adequately housed Applicants who live in a property that is adequate to meet their needs in terms of property type, size, and facilities. 3.10.2. Supported Housing/Hostels Applicants in supported housing/hostels and undergoing a resettlement programme and either not yet ready to move on or not engaging fully with the programme (based on the required evidence from an accredited supporting agency) or Applicants in supported housing/hostels who do not participate in the hostel move on agreement. 3.10.3. Deliberate worsening of circumstances and becoming homeless intentionally Applicants who are assessed by the council as having created or worsened their housing circumstances through their own actions or omissions, including those found to be intentionally homeless under homelessness legislation. This includes applicants who would otherwise be in a priority band. Examples: An applicant giving up accommodation that was suitable or more suitable for them than the accommodation they have moved into and which it was reasonable to continue to occupy. An applicant creating overcrowding by allowing family and/or friends to move into their home, which has worsened their housing situation. An applicant moving into a property that was unsuitable for their household needs from the outset. An applicant being unable to continue to occupy accommodation due to their deliberate action or omission. Homeowners who have transferred or gifted their property to another person. Applicants who have dispersed or deprived themselves of assets or capital which could have reasonably been used to secure housing. Unreasonably failing to follow advice given by the council in order to prevent homelessness. These are examples and this list is not exhaustive. There is no time limit on the imposition of standard band on these grounds. 4. Methods of assessment 4.1. Reduced preference 4.1.1. Section 166A(5) of the Housing Act 1996, as amended by the Homelessness Act 2002, allows allocation schemes to give reduced preference where the behaviour of an applicant (or member of their household) affects their suitability to be a tenant. 4.1.2. In such circumstances, where tenancy conditions have been breached, an assessment will be made as to whether the applicant’s behaviour merits their not qualifying for Home Options or whether an application can be taken and reduced preference applied. 4.1.3. An applicant will be given reduced preference if the council is satisfied they or a household member owes housing related debts or who has failed to maintain a rented property in a proper and reasonable condition. 4.1.4. Housing related debt includes but is not limited to: Any current or former tenant rent arrears or charges for use and occupation owed to any local authority, registered provider or private sector landlord. Unpaid sundry debts owing to any local authority, registered provider or private sector landlord, including rechargeable debts or court costs. Any tenancy deposit or rent in advance loans provided by the council that remain unpaid; or tenancy deposit guarantees that have been honoured by the council and remain unpaid. Outstanding council tax debts. Outstanding re-chargeable repairs. Current and former housing related service charge arrears. Temporary accommodation charge arrears where that temporary accommodation was provided by the council. Any court costs incurred by the council or a housing association associated with any of the above debts 4.1.5. In exceptional circumstances, applicants will be given additional preference despite meeting one of the criteria outlined above. Examples of where this may be appropriate are: Where a scheme landlord seeks discretion as current rent arrears are caused by welfare reform due to under-occupation and the applicant is seeking to downsize, is keeping to a repayment arrangement and is working with the landlord to address arrears.
